subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define sociology.
answer_html:
Definition Sociology is the scientific study of society – of human social relationships, groups, institutions and social behaviour.

Points to remember

  1. The word comes from the Latin socius (companion, society) and the Greek logos (study or science)
  2. The term was coined by Auguste Comte (1838), called the "father of sociology"
  3. MacIver and Page: sociology is about social relationships – "the network of relationships we call society"
  4. Ginsberg: sociology is the study of human interactions and interrelations, their conditions and consequences
  5. It studies how society influences people and how people shape society

subject: Applied Sociology
question: List the scope of sociology in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Sociology helps the nurse see the patient as a member of a family, community and culture, not only as a case.

Scope of sociology in nursing

  1. Understanding the social and cultural background of patients and families
  2. Studying the social causes of disease – poverty, overcrowding, illiteracy, addictions
  3. Community health nursing – knowing community structure, leaders and resources
  4. Understanding the hospital as a social institution and the roles of the health team
  5. Social problems – child labour, dowry, domestic violence, substance abuse
  6. Rehabilitation of patients and their return to society
  7. Planning and implementing health programmes acceptable to people

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the importance (significance) of sociology in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing deals with people, and people live in families, communities and cultures. Sociology gives the nurse knowledge of these social forces, so that care becomes holistic – meeting the patient's social needs along with physical and psychological needs.

1. Understanding the patient as a social being

  • Every patient belongs to a family, caste, class, religion and community
  • Knowing these helps the nurse understand the patient's behaviour, beliefs and expectations

2. Understanding social causes of disease

  • Many diseases have social roots – poverty, malnutrition, overcrowding, poor sanitation, illiteracy, addictions and unhealthy customs
  • Sociology helps nurses identify these causes and plan prevention

3. Culture and health practices

  • Food habits, taboos in pregnancy, home deliveries, beliefs about illness, use of traditional healers
  • The nurse learns to give culturally sensitive care without hurting beliefs

4. Family and health

  • The family is the basic unit of care in India – it decides about treatment and looks after the sick
  • Sociology helps the nurse involve the family in care and health education

5. Community health nursing

  • Knowledge of rural, urban and tribal communities, their structure, leaders, groups and resources
  • Helps in community diagnosis, home visits and organising health programmes

6. Hospital as a social system

  • The hospital is a social institution with roles, status and authority
  • Understanding group dynamics improves teamwork and the nurse–patient relationship

7. Social problems

  • Child labour, dowry, domestic violence, substance abuse, HIV/AIDS, problems of the elderly and disabled
  • The nurse can identify, counsel, refer and help prevent them

8. Rehabilitation and social welfare

  • Helps the nurse guide patients to social welfare schemes (Ayushman Bharat, old-age pensions, disability benefits) and support their return to normal life

9. Health education and change

  • Knowing how people accept new ideas helps in planning effective health education and acting as a change agent

10. Professional growth

  • Understanding social change, legislation and the status of women helps nurses develop the profession

Conclusion Sociology helps nurses understand patients in their social setting, identify social causes of disease and give holistic, culturally acceptable care in hospital and community.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define sociology. Explain its nature, scope and importance in nursing. (2 + 3 + 2 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Sociology is the science of society – the systematic study of human social relationships, groups, institutions and social behaviour
  • The word was coined by Auguste Comte in 1838 from the Latin socius (companion) and the Greek logos (study); Comte is known as the father of sociology
  • MacIver and Page: "Sociology is about social relationships, the network of relationship we call society"
  • Ginsberg: "Sociology is the study of human interactions and interrelations, their conditions and consequences"

(b) Nature of sociology (3 marks)

  1. A social science – it studies human society, not physical or natural phenomena
  2. A categorical (positive) science, not normative – it studies society as it is, not as it ought to be; it does not judge right or wrong
  3. A pure science – its aim is to gain knowledge; the application of this knowledge (e.g. in nursing or social work) is applied sociology
  4. An abstract science – it studies patterns of social relationships, not particular events or persons
  5. A generalising science – it makes general statements about society from the study of many cases
  6. Both rational and empirical – it uses reasoning and observation of facts
  7. An independent science – it has its own subject matter and methods (observation, surveys, case studies, interviews)

(c) Scope of sociology (2 marks) There are two main views:

  1. Formal (specialistic) school – led by Georg Simmel and Max Weber
    • Sociology should study only the forms of social relationships (cooperation, competition, conflict, domination), not their content
  2. Synthetic school – led by Emile Durkheim, Hobhouse and Sorokin
    • Sociology should be a general science that studies society as a whole and the relationship between all its parts

Main fields of sociological study

  • Social structure – groups, institutions, communities
  • Social processes – cooperation, competition, conflict, socialisation
  • Social change and social problems
  • Culture, family, marriage, religion, education, economy, politics
  • Branches: rural sociology, urban sociology, medical sociology, sociology of health, clinical sociology

(d) Importance of sociology in nursing (3 marks)

  1. Holistic care – understanding the patient as a member of a family and community, with social and cultural needs
  2. Social causes of disease – poverty, malnutrition, poor housing and sanitation, illiteracy and addictions
  3. Culture-sensitive care – respecting beliefs, food habits and practices; modifying harmful customs tactfully
  4. Role of family – involving the family in care, decisions and rehabilitation
  5. Community health nursing – understanding rural, urban and tribal communities, leaders and resources for health programmes
  6. Hospital as a social institution – roles, status, communication and teamwork
  7. Social problems – identifying and helping victims of domestic violence, child abuse, substance abuse
  8. Social welfare and rehabilitation – guiding patients to government schemes and community support
  9. Health education and change – knowing how people accept new practices helps the nurse act as a change agent
  10. Research – sociological methods (surveys, interviews) are used in nursing research

Relationship of sociology with other sciences

  • Psychology – studies the individual mind and behaviour; sociology studies groups and society; both meet in social psychology
  • Anthropology – studies human culture, especially of simple and tribal societies
  • Economics – studies production and distribution of wealth; poverty and unemployment are social as well as economic problems
  • Political science – studies the state and government; laws and policies shape society
  • Medicine and nursing – the social causes of disease (poverty, illiteracy, customs) are studied in medical sociology

Methods of sociology

  • Observation (including participant observation), survey and questionnaire, interview, case study, comparative method, historical method and statistical method

Example of applying sociology in nursing

  • A child from a migrant labourer's family is repeatedly admitted with diarrhoea. A nurse who understands sociology looks beyond the illness – at the family's poverty, slum housing, lack of safe water and the mother's long working hours – and plans health education, links the family with the anganwadi and the urban health centre, and checks immunisation.

Conclusion Sociology is the science of society. Its knowledge of groups, culture, family and social problems helps nurses give holistic, culturally appropriate care and work effectively in the community.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Name the pioneers of sociology and their contributions.
answer_html:
Introduction Sociology developed as a separate science in the 19th century. Its main pioneers are:

  1. Auguste Comte (France) – the "father of sociology"; coined the term "sociology" (1838); gave the law of three stages (theological, metaphysical, positive) and positivism
  2. Herbert Spencer (England) – compared society to a living organism; theory of social evolution
  3. Émile Durkheim (France) – social facts, division of labour, and a famous study of suicide as a social phenomenon
  4. Max Weber (Germany) – social action, bureaucracy, and religion and the economy
  5. Karl Marx (Germany) – class struggle and conflict theory

Indian pioneers

  • G. S. Ghurye – father of Indian sociology; studies of caste
  • M. N. Srinivas – Sanskritisation, dominant caste, westernisation

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What is medical sociology?
answer_html:
Definition Medical sociology (sociology of health and illness) is the branch of sociology that studies the social causes and consequences of health and illness and the social organisation of health care.

Two approaches (Robert Straus)

  • Sociology in medicine – applied studies that help solve health problems (e.g. social causes of disease)
  • Sociology of medicine – studies medicine and hospitals as social institutions

Scope

  1. Social factors in disease – poverty, culture, occupation, lifestyle
  2. Illness behaviour and the sick role (Talcott Parsons)
  3. Doctor–patient and nurse–patient relationships
  4. The hospital as a social organisation
  5. Inequalities in health and health care; stigma

Importance: helps nurses give holistic, culturally appropriate care.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the relationship of sociology with other social sciences.
answer_html:
Introduction Sociology is the general science of society – it studies all aspects of social life, while each of the other social sciences studies one particular aspect. They depend on one another, borrow concepts from each other and together give a complete picture of human life.

1. Sociology and psychology

  • Psychology studies the individual's mind and behaviour; sociology studies groups and society
  • Individual behaviour is shaped by society, and society is made up of individuals
  • Social psychology is the bridge between them – it studies attitudes, prejudice, leadership and group behaviour

2. Sociology and anthropology

  • Anthropology studies human beings – their origin, physical features and culture, especially in simple and tribal societies
  • Sociology studies mainly modern, complex societies
  • They are often called "twin sisters"; sociology borrows the concepts of culture and kinship from anthropology

3. Sociology and economics

  • Economics studies the production, distribution and consumption of wealth
  • Economic factors – poverty, unemployment, industrialisation – shape social life; social factors such as caste, family and values influence economic behaviour
  • Economic sociology links the two

4. Sociology and political science

  • Political science studies the state, government, power and laws
  • Laws change social institutions (e.g. laws on dowry and child marriage); social forces such as caste and religion influence voting and politics – political sociology

5. Sociology and history

  • History records past events in order of time; sociology studies present society and uses history to understand social change
  • Sociology without history has no roots, and history without sociology lacks meaning

6. Sociology and medicine and nursing

  • Medical sociology studies the social causes of disease and the organisation of health care
  • Nursing applies sociology in community health, family care and culturally sensitive care

Differences in brief

Science Main focus
Sociology society as a whole, social relationships
Psychology individual mind and behaviour
Anthropology human beings and culture, especially simple societies
Economics wealth and economic activity
Political science state, power and government
History past events

Conclusion Sociology is closely related to psychology, anthropology, economics, political science, history and medicine; each studies one part of human life, and together they help the nurse understand the patient as a member of society.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain social isolation.
answer_html:
Definition Social isolation is a condition in which a person or group has little or no contact or communication with others in society.

Types and causes

  1. Physical isolation – living in a remote area, prison, hospital isolation ward, bedridden or housebound
  2. Social or cultural isolation – due to caste discrimination, stigma (leprosy, HIV, mental illness), language barriers, migration
  3. Personal isolation – shyness, depression, old age, loss of a spouse

Effects

  • Loneliness, depression, poor self-esteem and poor health
  • In children – delayed social and language development

Nursing role: identify isolated patients (elderly, chronically ill), encourage family visits and group activities, fight stigma.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define socialisation and name its agencies.
answer_html:
Definition Socialisation is the process by which an individual learns the culture, norms, values and behaviour of his society and becomes a functioning member of it. It is a lifelong process that turns a biological being into a social being.

Agencies of socialisation

  1. Family – the first and most important agency
  2. Peer group – friends of the same age
  3. School and teachers
  4. Religion
  5. Mass media – television, internet, social media
  6. Workplace and occupation
  7. State and law

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define social change.
answer_html:
Definition Social change means changes in the structure and functioning of society – in social relationships, institutions, values and ways of life – over time.

MacIver and Page: social change is change in social relationships.

Examples in India

  1. Shift from joint to nuclear families
  2. Increasing education and employment of women
  3. Weakening of caste restrictions in cities
  4. Use of mobile phones and the internet
  5. Rise in institutional deliveries

Factors: technology, economic development, education, mass media, legislation, urbanisation, population changes and contact with other cultures.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Differentiate between primary and secondary groups.
answer_html:
Introduction The terms primary group and secondary group were introduced by C. H. Cooley.

Primary group Secondary group
small in size large in size
face-to-face, intimate relations indirect, formal, impersonal relations
permanent, long-lasting may be temporary
relationships are an end in themselves relationships are a means to an end
informal control (love, ridicule) formal control (rules, laws)
e.g. family, close friends, neighbours e.g. trade union, political party, hospital staff association

Importance: the primary group is the "nursery of human nature" – it shapes personality.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Differentiate between society and community.
answer_html:
Introduction Society and community are basic concepts of sociology. They are related but not the same.

  • Society – a web of social relationships (MacIver and Page)
  • Community – a group of people living in a particular area and sharing a common life and a feeling of belonging ("we-feeling")

Differences

Point Society Community
Meaning network of social relationships group of people living in a definite locality
Nature abstract – relationships cannot be seen concrete – people and place can be seen
Locality no definite territory definite geographical area
Community sentiment not essential essential – "we-feeling"
Size wider; may include many communities smaller; part of a society
Interests may have both common and different interests common interests and common life
Membership voluntary, by relationships by birth or residence
Likeness involves both likeness and difference mostly likeness
Formation develops gradually develops spontaneously in a locality
Example Indian society a village, town or tribal community

Elements of community

  1. A group of people
  2. A definite locality
  3. Community sentiment (we-feeling, belonging)
  4. Common life and culture
  5. Spontaneous growth and permanence
  6. A name

Nursing importance

  • Community health nursing works with communities – their leaders, customs and resources
  • Knowing the community sentiment helps in community participation for health programmes (Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committees)

Characteristics of society

  • An abstract web of social relationships (MacIver and Page)
  • Based on likeness and also differences among members
  • Involves cooperation as well as conflict
  • Interdependence of members
  • Has its own culture and is dynamic (keeps changing)

Example: "Indian society" is an abstract network of relationships, while "the village of Mohgaon" is a concrete community with a definite area and a feeling of belonging.

Conclusion Society is a wide, abstract network of relationships, while a community is a concrete group of people sharing a locality and a sense of belonging.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Describe the social processes.
answer_html:
Introduction Social processes are the ways in which individuals and groups interact and establish relationships. Ginsberg describes them as the various modes of interaction between individuals or groups, including cooperation and conflict, social differentiation and integration. They are of two types – associative (bring people together) and dissociative (keep them apart).

A. Associative processes

1. Cooperation

  • Working together for a common goal
  • The most basic social process; needed for family life, work and community development
  • Types: direct (doing things together) and indirect (division of labour)
  • Example: the health team working together to save a patient

2. Accommodation

  • Adjustment between conflicting individuals or groups so that they can live together peacefully, even though differences remain
  • Forms: compromise, arbitration, tolerance, conciliation
  • Example: a newly married woman adjusting to her husband's family; a patient adjusting to hospital routine

3. Assimilation

  • A slow process by which individuals or groups of different cultures merge into one, adopting a common culture
  • Example: migrants gradually adopting the language and customs of a city

4. Acculturation

  • Taking over some traits of another culture through contact, while keeping one's own culture

B. Dissociative processes

1. Competition

  • A struggle to obtain something limited (jobs, seats, prizes) without using force
  • Impersonal and continuous; can be healthy (motivates) or harmful
  • Example: competition for admission to nursing colleges

2. Conflict

  • A direct struggle in which parties try to defeat each other, sometimes by force or violence
  • Personal, intermittent
  • Example: communal riots, family quarrels, strikes

3. Isolation

  • Lack of social contact – may be physical or social

Importance for nurses

  • Cooperation is the basis of teamwork in hospitals
  • Nurses help patients accommodate to illness and hospitalisation
  • Recognising and resolving conflict improves the work environment

Conclusion Social processes are patterns of interaction – associative processes unite people and dissociative processes divide them; a nurse should promote cooperation and accommodation.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: List the major problems of urban communities (cities).
answer_html:
Introduction Urbanisation is the growth of towns and cities and the movement of people from rural to urban areas. India's cities are growing rapidly, and this growth brings many social and health problems.

1. Overcrowding and housing shortage

  • Too many people in a small area; high cost of housing
  • Growth of slums with poor housing, no ventilation and no sanitation

2. Environmental pollution

  • Air pollution from vehicles and industries – respiratory diseases, asthma
  • Water pollution and shortage of safe drinking water
  • Noise pollution
  • Problems of solid waste disposal and drainage

3. Traffic congestion and road accidents

  • Major cause of death and disability in young adults

4. Unemployment and poverty

  • Migrants from villages often get only unskilled, insecure jobs; many live below the poverty line

5. Crime and delinquency

  • Theft, robbery, violence, juvenile delinquency, gangs

6. Substance abuse and prostitution

  • Alcoholism, drug addiction and prostitution are more common in cities

7. Breakdown of family and social ties

  • Nuclear families, loneliness, neglect of the elderly, stress
  • Impersonal relationships; weak social control

8. Health problems

  • Lifestyle diseases – diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, obesity, cancer
  • Communicable diseases in slums – TB, diarrhoea, dengue, malaria
  • Mental stress, depression and suicide
  • Occupational diseases

9. Problems of migrants

  • Lack of identity documents, housing and access to health care

Nursing role

  • Urban health services – Urban Primary Health Centres, Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
  • Health education on sanitation, safe water, lifestyle changes and road safety
  • Screening for non-communicable diseases
  • Special attention to slum dwellers, migrants and the elderly

10. Inadequate water supply and sanitation

  • Shortage of safe drinking water, open drains and garbage heaps in slums, leading to diarrhoea, typhoid, hepatitis, dengue and malaria

11. Stress and lifestyle diseases

  • Fast life, long working hours, sedentary jobs and junk food increase hypertension, diabetes, obesity, depression and anxiety

12. Poor health care access for the urban poor

  • Slum dwellers often cannot afford private care; the National Urban Health Mission provides urban primary health centres and urban ASHAs for them

Conclusion Rapid urbanisation in India has created overcrowding, slums, pollution, accidents, crime, broken social ties and lifestyle diseases; urban health programmes and health education help tackle them.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain social change and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Society is never static. Social change is the alteration in social structure, relationships, institutions, values and ways of life over time. MacIver and Page define it as change in social relationships.

1. Characteristics

  • Universal – occurs in every society
  • Continuous, but its speed differs
  • Community change, not individual change
  • May be planned or unplanned
  • Its direction and results cannot be predicted exactly

2. Factors (causes) of social change

  1. Technological – machines, transport, mobile phones, internet, medical technology
  2. Economic – industrialisation, new occupations, employment of women
  3. Demographic – population growth, migration, longer life span
  4. Cultural – new ideas, values and beliefs; contact with other cultures
  5. Educational – education changes attitudes and aspirations
  6. Political and legal – laws against untouchability, dowry, child marriage; reservation policies
  7. Geographical – floods, droughts, earthquakes
  8. Mass media – spreads new ideas quickly

3. Examples of social change in India

  • Joint families giving way to nuclear families
  • Rising education and employment of women
  • Increasing inter-caste marriages in cities
  • Shift from home births to institutional deliveries
  • Digital health services and telemedicine

4. Effects on health

  • Positive: better health services, education, awareness, longer life
  • Negative: stress, lifestyle diseases, loneliness of the elderly, addictions

5. Role of the nurse in social change

  • Change agent – introduces healthy practices (hand washing, breastfeeding, immunisation) in the community
  • Health educator – removes harmful beliefs tactfully
  • Adapting to change – learns new technology and new treatment methods
  • Supporting people affected by change – elderly living alone, migrants
  • Participating in planning of health programmes and policies
  • Role model for healthy living

Theories (patterns) of social change

  • Evolutionary – society changes gradually from simple to complex forms
  • Cyclical – societies rise and decline in cycles
  • Conflict – change results from conflict between groups (Karl Marx)

Resistance to change

  • People resist change because of habits, fear of the unknown, vested interests, religious beliefs and lack of information
  • Resistance is reduced by education, participation of people, demonstration of benefits and involvement of community leaders – for example, involving religious leaders in the polio campaign

Conclusion Social change is a continuous process driven by technology, economy, education and law; the nurse both adapts to change and guides people towards healthy change.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define social group. Explain the process of socialisation. Discuss the functions of institutions. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
(a) Social group (2 marks) Definition

  • MacIver and Page: a social group is "any collection of human beings who are brought into human relationships with one another"
  • In simple words, a group is two or more people who interact, share common interests and have a sense of belonging

Characteristics of a social group

  • Collection of individuals with mutual interaction
  • Sense of unity and "we-feeling"
  • Common interests and goals
  • Norms that guide members' behaviour
  • Some stability

Classification

  • Primary and secondary groups (C. H. Cooley) – family vs trade union
  • In-group and out-group (W. G. Sumner) – "we" vs "they"
  • Formal and informal groups; voluntary and involuntary groups
  • Reference group (Merton) – a group whose standards a person uses to judge himself

(b) Process of socialisation (4 marks) Definition: socialisation is the process by which an individual learns the culture, norms, values and roles of his society and becomes a social being. It begins at birth and continues throughout life.

1. Stages of socialisation

  • Infancy (oral stage) – the baby depends totally on the mother; learns trust, feeding habits and responding to care
  • Early childhood (anal stage) – toilet training, learning simple rules, language, "yes" and "no"
  • Childhood (school age) – learns sex roles, discipline, cooperation, school rules and moral values
  • Adolescence – desire for independence; peer group is very important; learns adult roles and values
  • Adulthood – occupational roles, marriage and parenthood (secondary socialisation)
  • Old age – adjusting to retirement and loss of roles

2. Theories of how the self develops

  • C. H. Cooley – "looking-glass self": we form an idea of ourselves from how we think others see and judge us
  • G. H. Mead – "I and Me": the self develops through social interaction and role-taking (play and games)
  • Freud – personality develops through the interaction of id, ego and superego

3. Types of socialisation

  • Primary – in childhood, mainly by the family
  • Secondary – later in life, by school, peers, workplace
  • Anticipatory – learning the role one expects to take (a nursing student learning the nurse's role)
  • Re-socialisation – learning new values after a major change (prison, migration, long hospitalisation)

4. Agencies of socialisation

  • Family – the first and most powerful agency; teaches language, habits, values
  • Peer group – friendship, cooperation, independence
  • School – knowledge, discipline, citizenship
  • Religion – moral values
  • Mass media – attitudes, lifestyle
  • Workplace – occupational roles and ethics
  • State – laws and rights

(c) Functions of institutions (4 marks) Definition: a social institution is an organised, established system of norms and procedures that satisfies a basic need of society (MacIver: established forms or conditions of procedure characteristic of group activity).

Major institutions: family, marriage, religion, education, economic, political and health institutions.

General functions

  1. Satisfy basic needs of society – reproduction, food, order, knowledge
  2. Regulate behaviour – through rules and norms (social control)
  3. Transmit culture from one generation to the next
  4. Assign roles and status to individuals
  5. Provide stability and unity in society
  6. Simplify behaviour – people know how to act in situations

Functions of individual institutions

  • Family – reproduction, child rearing, socialisation, affection, economic support, care of the sick and elderly
  • Marriage – regulates sex life, gives legitimacy to children, establishes the family
  • Religion – moral values, unity, comfort in crisis, social control
  • Education – knowledge, skills, values, preparation for occupation, social mobility
  • Economic institutions – production and distribution of goods and services, employment
  • Political institutions (state) – law and order, protection, welfare, rights
  • Health institutions (hospitals) – prevention and treatment of disease, health promotion, training, research

Nursing importance

  • Groups (families, self-help groups, support groups) are used in health education and rehabilitation
  • Professional socialisation shapes nursing students into nurses
  • The hospital is an institution with its own roles, norms and hierarchy

Conclusion A social group is a collection of interacting individuals with a sense of unity; socialisation turns individuals into members of society through stages and agencies; and institutions meet society's basic needs, regulate behaviour and transmit culture.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Describe the characteristics of rural, urban and tribal communities and their major health problems. (3 + 3 + 2 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction India is a land of villages, growing cities and many tribal groups. Each type of community has its own social structure and health problems, and a nurse must understand them to plan appropriate care.

(a) Rural community (3 marks) Characteristics

  1. Small size and low population density
  2. Agriculture is the main occupation; dependence on nature
  3. Homogeneity – people share similar culture, beliefs and occupations
  4. Primary relationships – face-to-face, intimate, everyone knows everyone
  5. Joint family system is still common
  6. Caste system is strong; traditional leadership (panchayat, elders)
  7. Simplicity, religiosity and traditionalism; slower acceptance of change
  8. Strong community feeling and informal social control

Major health problems

  • Communicable diseases – diarrhoea, TB, malaria, worm infestations, typhoid
  • Malnutrition and anaemia, especially in women and children
  • Lack of safe water and sanitation (improving under the Swachh Bharat Mission)
  • Maternal and child health problems; home deliveries in remote areas
  • Poor access to health facilities and doctors
  • Occupational hazards – pesticide poisoning, snake bite, injuries from farm machines, heat stroke
  • Superstitions and use of untrained healers
  • Alcoholism and tobacco use

(b) Urban community (3 marks) Characteristics

  1. Large size and high density of population
  2. Non-agricultural occupations – industry, trade, services
  3. Heterogeneity – people of different religions, castes, languages and cultures
  4. Secondary relationships – impersonal, formal
  5. Nuclear families
  6. Social mobility – occupation and wealth matter more than caste
  7. Formal social control (police, law)
  8. Faster social change; more individualism

Major health problems

  • Overcrowding and slums – TB, respiratory infections, diarrhoea
  • Pollution – air, water and noise
  • Lifestyle diseases – diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, obesity, cancer
  • Road traffic accidents
  • Stress, depression, substance abuse and suicide
  • Mosquito-borne diseases (dengue, malaria) in poorly drained areas

(c) Tribal community (2 marks) Characteristics

  • Live in forests and hilly areas, often isolated
  • Distinct language, dialect, customs and religion
  • Depend on forests, hunting, shifting cultivation and labour
  • Strong group feeling; tribal councils
  • Simple economy; low literacy

Major health problems

  • Malaria, TB, skin infections
  • Malnutrition and anaemia
  • Sickle cell disease in many tribal groups of central and western India
  • High maternal and infant mortality
  • Alcoholism, tobacco use
  • Poor access to health services; reliance on traditional healers

(d) Role of the nurse (2 marks)

  • Community diagnosis – understand the community's structure, leaders and health problems
  • Rural: immunisation, antenatal care, nutrition, sanitation, safe water, malaria control; work with ASHA and Anganwadi workers
  • Urban: screening for non-communicable diseases, slum health, road safety and mental health education
  • Tribal: culturally sensitive approach, mobile health units, sickle cell screening, gaining the trust of tribal leaders
  • Link people to government schemes and health programmes

Comparison of rural, urban and tribal communities

Point Rural Urban Tribal
Size and density small, low density large, high density small, scattered
Occupation agriculture industry, trade, services forest produce, hunting, shifting cultivation
Family joint family common nuclear family common clan-based
Social control informal – customs, panchayat formal – police, courts tribal council, customs
Relationships close, personal impersonal, formal very close, kinship-based
Health services sub-centres, PHCs, ASHA hospitals, urban PHCs few, difficult to reach

Health services for each

  • Rural: sub-centres and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, PHCs, CHCs, ASHAs and anganwadi workers under the National Rural Health Mission
  • Urban: urban PHCs, urban CHCs and urban ASHAs under the National Urban Health Mission
  • Tribal and hilly areas: relaxed population norms – a sub-centre for about 3,000 people and a PHC for about 20,000 (against 5,000 and 30,000 in the plains); mobile medical units

Conclusion Rural communities are small, homogeneous and agricultural; urban communities are large, heterogeneous and industrial; tribal communities are isolated with distinct cultures. Each faces different health problems, and nursing care must be planned to suit each setting.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Differentiate between association and institution.
answer_html:
Introduction Both are parts of social structure, but they are different.

Association Institution
an organised group of people formed to pursue a common interest (MacIver) an established set of rules and procedures that governs group activity
concrete – has members abstract – a system of norms
formed deliberately evolves gradually over time
may be temporary relatively permanent
one joins it one follows it
has a name, office-bearers and structure has customs, symbols and traditions

Examples (association – institution)

  • Family – marriage
  • College – education
  • Hospital – health care (medicine)
  • Trained Nurses' Association of India, trade union, club – professional ethics, labour laws

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define urbanisation. Give its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Urbanisation is the process by which an increasing proportion of the population comes to live in towns and cities, together with the spread of the urban way of life. About 31% of India's population lived in urban areas at the 2011 Census, and the share is rising.

Causes

  1. Industrialisation – factories and services create jobs in cities
  2. Rural-to-urban migration:
    • push factors – poverty, unemployment, small landholdings, drought, caste oppression
    • pull factors – jobs, higher wages, education, hospitals, amenities
  3. Natural increase of the urban population
  4. Better transport and communication
  5. Government policies – smart cities, industrial corridors
  6. Expansion of city limits to include nearby villages

Applied: rapid urbanisation leads to slums, overcrowding, pollution and lifestyle diseases.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define migration. Give its types and causes.
answer_html:
Definition Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to settle there temporarily or permanently.

Types

  1. Internal (within the country) and international (emigration and immigration)
  2. Rural to urban, rural to rural, urban to urban, urban to rural
  3. Seasonal or temporary – e.g. sugarcane cutters and brick-kiln workers – and permanent
  4. Voluntary and forced (displacement by dams, disasters, conflict)

Causes

  • Push factors – poverty, unemployment, drought, natural disasters, conflict
  • Pull factors – employment, higher wages, education, health care, urban facilities
  • Marriage – the main reason for the migration of women in India

Health importance: migrants often live in slums, miss immunisation and health care, and are at higher risk of TB, HIV and malnutrition – they need special outreach.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the relationship between the individual and society.
answer_html:
Introduction Aristotle said, "Man is a social animal." The individual and society are interdependent, like two sides of the same coin – society is made up of individuals, and the individual becomes truly human only in society.

1. Theories of the relationship

  • Social contract theory (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau) – individuals created society by an agreement, to gain protection and order; criticised because there is no historical evidence for such a contract
  • Organismic theory (Herbert Spencer) – society is like a living organism and individuals are like its cells, each with a function; criticised because individuals have their own consciousness and will
  • Group mind theory (Durkheim, McDougall) – society has a collective conscience that is more than the sum of individual minds
  • Modern view – the individual and society develop together through social interaction; neither can exist without the other

2. The individual depends on society

  • Survival and basic needs – a human infant is helpless and depends on others for food, shelter and protection
  • Socialisation – language, culture, values and habits are learned only in society
  • Evidence – feral children such as Kamala and Amala, found living with wolves near Midnapore (Bengal) in 1920, could not walk upright or speak and behaved like animals; they showed that human qualities develop only through social contact
  • Personality, identity, status and roles are given by society
  • Security, cooperation, education and health care are provided by society

3. Society depends on individuals

  • Society consists of individuals; their cooperation keeps institutions working
  • Individuals transmit culture to the next generation
  • Individuals bring social change – reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Mahatma Jyotiba Phule and Savitribai Phule, Dr B. R. Ambedkar, and Florence Nightingale in nursing

4. Conflict between the individual and society

  • When individual desires clash with social norms, deviance results, and society uses social control
  • A balance is needed between individual freedom and social welfare – rights go with duties

5. Importance in nursing

  • The patient is a member of a family and community; social support speeds recovery
  • Health behaviour – diet, addiction, use of health services – is shaped by society
  • The nurse acts as a change agent and works with families and communities

Conclusion The individual and society are inseparable: the individual receives survival, culture and personality from society, and society is maintained and changed by individuals; good nursing care considers the patient within his social setting.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain personal disorganisation – its causes, forms and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Personal disorganisation is a condition in which an individual fails to adjust to the social environment and behaves in ways that deviate from accepted social norms, harming himself, his family or society (Elliott and Merrill). Personal and social disorganisation are closely linked – each can lead to the other.

1. Causes

  • Individual factors – physical or mental illness, disability, low intelligence, emotional immaturity, unresolved frustration and conflict
  • Family factors – broken homes, divorce or death of a parent, domestic violence, neglect, too strict or too lenient discipline, alcoholic parents
  • Social factors – poverty, unemployment, slums, bad company, rapid social change, urbanisation and migration (loss of family support), cultural conflict, discrimination
  • Life crises – failure in examinations or business, loss of job or status, bereavement, debt

2. Forms (manifestations)

  • Alcoholism and drug addiction
  • Juvenile delinquency and crime
  • Suicidal behaviour
  • Gambling, vagrancy and beggary
  • Prostitution
  • Mental disorders – anxiety, depression, neurosis

3. Effects

  • Individual – ill health, loss of work, loss of self-respect
  • Family – quarrels, breakdown, neglect of children, financial loss
  • Society – crime, violence, loss of productivity, burden on services

4. Prevention

  • Strong family life and good parenting
  • Education and life-skills training for children and adolescents
  • Employment and poverty-alleviation programmes
  • Guidance and counselling in schools, colleges and workplaces
  • Recreation facilities and youth clubs
  • Early identification and treatment of mental illness and addiction
  • De-addiction and rehabilitation services; community support groups

5. Role of the nurse

  • Identify high-risk individuals – the unemployed, addicts, the bereaved, adolescents in difficulty
  • Listen, counsel and refer to counsellors, de-addiction centres or mental health services; for anyone in distress, give the Tele-MANAS helpline (14416)
  • Health education of families and communities; support family members
  • Take part in crisis intervention and rehabilitation

6. Personal and social disorganisation compared

Personal disorganisation Social disorganisation
failure of an individual to adjust breakdown of social order and institutions
seen as addiction, crime, mental disorder seen as weak families, corruption, riots, unrest
affects mainly the person and his family affects the whole community or society
  • Each can cause the other – a disorganised society produces disorganised individuals, and many such individuals weaken society

Conclusion Personal disorganisation is an individual's failure to adjust to social norms, caused by personal, family and social factors and seen as addiction, delinquency, crime and mental disorder; strong families, education, employment, counselling and early help prevent it.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the characteristics of culture.
answer_html:
Definition E. B. Tylor: culture is "that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society".

Characteristics of culture

  1. Learned – acquired through socialisation, not inherited biologically
  2. Shared – common to members of a group
  3. Transmitted from generation to generation – our "social heritage"
  4. Symbolic – based on language and symbols
  5. Dynamic – changes slowly over time
  6. Adaptive – helps people adjust to their environment
  7. Integrated – its parts are inter-related
  8. Varies from society to society
  9. Satisfies human needs

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Differentiate between culture and civilisation.
answer_html:
Introduction MacIver distinguished culture (what we are) from civilisation (what we use).

Culture Civilisation
refers to ends – values, beliefs, ideals, art, religion refers to means – tools, machines, technology
internal, non-material external, mostly material
difficult to measure can be measured (efficiency)
not always progressive always moves forward (advances)
cannot be borrowed easily without change can be borrowed easily (e.g. mobile phones)
expresses the inner life of a people serves practical needs

Example: a temple's spiritual meaning is culture; the construction technique is civilisation.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Describe the functions of culture.
answer_html:
Introduction Culture is the total way of life of a people – their knowledge, beliefs, customs, values, language, art and material objects. It is learned and shared, and it shapes almost everything we think and do.

Functions of culture

1. Makes man a social being

  • A child becomes "human" in the social sense by learning culture – language, manners, values
  • Without culture man would live only by instincts

2. Provides patterns of behaviour

  • Culture gives ready-made ways of behaving in different situations – greeting elders, eating, dressing, celebrating festivals
  • People know what is expected of them

3. Satisfies needs

  • Provides ways to satisfy biological needs (food, shelter, sex through marriage) and social needs (recognition, belonging)

4. Shapes personality

  • Values, attitudes and habits of individuals are moulded by culture
  • People of different cultures think and behave differently

5. Gives identity and unity

  • Common culture gives a sense of belonging and "we-feeling" to a group or nation
  • Festivals, language and customs unite people

6. Social control

  • Folkways, mores, customs and religion regulate behaviour
  • Approval and disapproval of society keep people within norms

7. Defines situations and meanings

  • Culture tells us what is good or bad, clean or unclean, normal or abnormal – including what is considered illness

8. Provides solutions to problems

  • Accumulated knowledge and tools help people adapt to their environment

9. Transmits social heritage

  • Knowledge and experience are passed on to the next generation, so each generation does not start afresh

10. Integrates society

  • Brings together the different parts of social life into a meaningful whole

Nursing importance

  • Patients' behaviour in illness, pain expression, diet and acceptance of treatment are shaped by culture
  • Nurses must give culturally sensitive care

Characteristics of culture (in brief)

  • Learnt (not inherited), shared, transmitted from generation to generation, symbolic (based on language), dynamic (changes over time), adaptive, integrated and varies from society to society

Example from health

  • Culture decides what a pregnant woman eats, where the delivery takes place, how a newborn is fed and how the family reacts to illness; the nurse must respect helpful practices and gently change harmful ones.

Conclusion Culture makes man a social being, guides behaviour, satisfies needs, shapes personality, unites the group and maintains social control.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the impact of culture on health.
answer_html:
Introduction Health and illness are not only biological. Culture decides what people eat, how they keep clean, what they believe causes disease, whom they consult when ill and how they behave in pregnancy, childbirth and death. A nurse must understand these influences to give effective care.

1. Food habits and nutrition

  • Vegetarianism, fasting during festivals, food taboos
  • Taboos in pregnancy – avoiding papaya, eggs or certain fruits; "eating less" to have a small baby → maternal anaemia and low birth weight
  • Discarding colostrum and giving prelacteal feeds (honey, water) in some communities → infections in newborns
  • Tobacco and betel chewing

2. Personal hygiene and sanitation

  • Bathing, hand washing and toilet habits vary
  • Open defecation (now reducing) spreads worm infestations and diarrhoea

3. Beliefs about the causes of disease

  • Evil eye, spirits, sin or punishment by gods – leads to delay in treatment and use of faith healers
  • Mental illness and epilepsy may be attributed to supernatural causes

4. Health-seeking behaviour

  • Preference for traditional healers, home remedies or AYUSH systems
  • Shame about certain illnesses (TB, leprosy, HIV, sexually transmitted infections) delays treatment

5. Marriage and family customs

  • Child marriage → teenage pregnancy, maternal and infant deaths
  • Consanguineous marriage → genetic disorders (thalassaemia, congenital anomalies)
  • Son preference → neglect of girls, sex-selective abortion, fall in child sex ratio
  • Large family size and short birth intervals

6. Childbirth and child-rearing practices

  • Home deliveries by untrained dais, unsafe cord care (applying cow dung or ash)
  • Oil massage, swaddling, branding as a treatment for illness

7. Attitude to the body and disability

  • Modesty may prevent women from seeking care from male doctors
  • Stigma towards disabled persons

8. Addictions and lifestyle

  • Alcohol and tobacco use linked to social customs and festivals
  • Modernisation has increased junk food, inactivity and lifestyle diseases

9. Positive cultural practices

  • Yoga, meditation, breastfeeding for a long time, joint family support for the sick and elderly, vegetarian diets

Nursing role (transcultural nursing)

  • Assess the patient's cultural beliefs and practices
  • Respect harmless practices; tactfully change harmful ones through health education
  • Avoid stereotyping and ethnocentrism (judging others by one's own culture)
  • Use the local language and involve community leaders

Conclusion Culture influences diet, hygiene, beliefs, health-seeking, marriage and childbirth; some practices protect health and others harm it, so nurses must give culturally sensitive care.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define culture. Describe the elements (components) of culture and explain transcultural nursing. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
(a) Definition of culture (2 marks)

  • E. B. Tylor (1871): "Culture is that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society"
  • Malinowski: culture is the handiwork of man and the medium through which he achieves his ends
  • In simple words, culture is the total, learned way of life of a group of people that is shared and passed from one generation to the next
  • Characteristics: learned, shared, transmitted, symbolic, dynamic, adaptive, integrated and different in different societies

(b) Elements (components) of culture (4 marks)

A. Material culture

  • All the tangible, man-made objects – houses, tools, clothes, utensils, vehicles, machines, medicines, hospitals
  • Changes faster than non-material culture

B. Non-material culture

  • The intangible parts – ideas, beliefs, values, norms, language, customs

Main elements of non-material culture

  1. Language and symbols
    • The chief means of communication and transmission of culture
    • Gestures, signs and symbols (the red cross, a wedding ring)
  2. Beliefs
    • Ideas that people accept as true – religious beliefs, beliefs about health and disease
  3. Values
    • Shared ideas about what is good, right and desirable – honesty, respect for elders, cleanliness
  4. Norms – rules of expected behaviour
    • Folkways – everyday customs (greeting with folded hands); mild disapproval if broken
    • Mores – norms with moral significance (not stealing, care of parents); strong disapproval if broken
    • Laws – formal norms enforced by the state
    • Customs, traditions and taboos
  5. Knowledge and technology
    • Accumulated information and skills (agriculture, medicine)
  6. Art, literature, music and religion – expressive culture

Cultural lag (Ogburn) – when material culture changes faster than non-material culture (e.g. technology changes quickly but attitudes change slowly).

(c) Transcultural nursing (4 marks) 1. Meaning

  • Transcultural nursing is the branch of nursing that focuses on the comparative study of cultures to understand similarities and differences in health beliefs and practices, and on providing culturally congruent (culture-appropriate) care
  • Developed by Madeleine Leininger (Culture Care Diversity and Universality theory)

2. Need in India

  • India has great diversity of religions, languages, castes, tribes and regional customs
  • Migration and medical tourism bring patients from many cultures

3. Key concepts

  • Cultural awareness – recognising one's own beliefs and biases
  • Cultural knowledge – learning about the beliefs and practices of other groups
  • Cultural sensitivity – respecting differences without judging
  • Cultural competence – the ability to provide effective care to people of all cultures
  • Avoid ethnocentrism (believing one's own culture is superior) and stereotyping

4. Leininger's three modes of nursing action

  • Culture care preservation – support beneficial practices (breastfeeding, family support, yoga)
  • Culture care accommodation (negotiation) – adjust care to fit harmless beliefs (allowing religious threads, providing vegetarian diet, female nurse for female patients)
  • Culture care repatterning – tactfully help patients change harmful practices (discarding colostrum, applying cow dung on the cord, prolonged fasting in diabetes)

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Carry out a cultural assessment – language, religion, diet, beliefs about illness, family roles, decision-makers
  • Communicate in the patient's language; use interpreters when needed
  • Respect privacy, modesty and religious practices (prayer times, fasting, rituals at death)
  • Plan diet according to cultural and religious preferences
  • Involve family and community leaders in health education
  • Explain procedures in a way that fits the patient's beliefs

Important cultural concepts

  • Cultural lag (W. F. Ogburn) – material culture (technology) changes faster than non-material culture (beliefs, values); e.g. modern hospitals are available, but some families still delay treatment because of old beliefs
  • Ethnocentrism – believing that one's own culture is superior and judging others by it; it leads to prejudice in nursing care
  • Cultural relativism – understanding a culture on its own terms, without judging it
  • Culture shock – confusion and anxiety on entering an unfamiliar culture; e.g. a nurse posted in a tribal area, or a patient from a village admitted to a big city hospital
  • Acculturation – adopting traits of another culture through continuous contact
  • Subculture – a group with distinct ways within a larger culture (tribal groups, slum dwellers, hospital staff)

Conclusion Culture is the learned, shared way of life of a people, made of material objects and non-material elements such as language, beliefs, values and norms. Transcultural nursing uses this understanding to give care that respects each patient's culture.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What is ethnocentrism? How does it differ from cultural relativism?
answer_html:
Ethnocentrism

  • The tendency to judge other cultures by the standards of one's own culture, believing one's own culture to be superior (term coined by W. G. Sumner)
  • Example: laughing at another community's food habits or rituals

Cultural relativism

  • The principle that every culture should be understood in its own context, without judging it by the standards of another culture (Franz Boas)
  • Example: understanding why a patient prefers home remedies or a female nurse

Differences

Ethnocentrism Cultural relativism
judges others by one's own culture understands others in their own setting
leads to prejudice and conflict leads to respect and tolerance
blocks communication helps communication

Nursing importance: nurses avoid ethnocentrism and practise cultural relativism to give culturally sensitive care.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What is culture shock?
answer_html:
Definition Culture shock is the feeling of confusion, anxiety, disorientation and helplessness experienced when a person enters an unfamiliar culture – a new country, region or environment (described by Kalervo Oberg).

Stages

  1. Honeymoon – excitement about the new place
  2. Crisis (frustration) – irritation, homesickness, confusion
  3. Adjustment – learns the new ways
  4. Adaptation – feels at home

Signs: homesickness, irritability, withdrawal, loss of appetite and sleep.

Examples

  • A rural or tribal patient admitted to a big city hospital
  • A nurse posted to another state

Nursing: orient the patient, speak in his language, respect customs and involve the family.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the evolution (development) of culture.
answer_html:
Introduction Culture is the total way of life of a people. It is not static – it has developed gradually over thousands of years, from simple to complex, and is passed on from generation to generation.

1. Stages of cultural evolution

  • L. H. Morgan described three broad stages – savagery, barbarism and civilisation
  • Old Stone Age (Palaeolithic) – hunting and food gathering; crude stone tools; discovery of fire; nomadic life in caves
  • New Stone Age (Neolithic) – agriculture, domestication of animals, pottery and permanent villages (the "Neolithic revolution")
  • Metal Age – copper, bronze and iron tools; trade; towns
  • Civilisation – writing, cities and organised government, e.g. the Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation in India
  • Industrial revolution – machines, factories and urbanisation
  • Modern information age – computers, the internet, globalisation and digital health

2. Processes by which culture develops

  • Discovery – finding something that already exists (fire, medicinal plants)
  • Invention – creating something new (the wheel, vaccines, the X-ray)
  • Diffusion – spread of cultural traits from one society to another (tea drinking, the English language, modern medicine)
  • Accumulation – new traits are added to the old; culture grows like a store
  • Acculturation – exchange of traits through long contact between groups
  • Material culture changes faster than non-material culture, which can create a lag

3. Characteristics of cultural evolution

  • Gradual and continuous
  • Cumulative – builds on the past
  • From simple to complex
  • Influenced by environment, technology and contact with other cultures

4. Importance in nursing

  • Health practices have evolved from magico-religious beliefs (illness as punishment or evil spirits) to scientific medicine
  • Traditional beliefs still exist alongside modern medicine – nurses must understand both and use health education to bring change
  • Nursing itself has evolved from religious charity to a scientific profession

5. Theories of cultural evolution (in brief)

  • Unilinear (classical) evolution – Morgan and Tylor: all societies pass through the same stages in the same order
  • Diffusionism – culture spread outwards from a few centres of invention
  • Multilinear evolution – Julian Steward: societies follow different paths depending on their environment and technology
  • Modern view – cultures change through a combination of internal invention and outside contact

Conclusion Culture has evolved from the hunting-gathering stage through agriculture, metals, civilisation and industry to the modern information age, through discovery, invention, diffusion and accumulation; understanding this helps nurses respect traditional beliefs while promoting scientific health practices.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain cultural diversity and uniformity in India.
answer_html:
Introduction India is known for "unity in diversity". Cultural diversity means the variety of languages, religions, customs and ways of life found among its people; cultural uniformity (unity) means the common elements that bind them together as one nation.

A. Cultural diversity

  1. Racial – people of many racial stocks live in India
  2. Linguistic – 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution and hundreds of dialects
  3. Religious – Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism, Judaism and tribal religions
  4. Caste and tribe – thousands of castes and sub-castes; more than 700 Scheduled Tribes
  5. Regional customs – differences in food, dress, festivals, marriage customs and kinship; e.g. matrilineal Khasi and Garo communities of Meghalaya
  6. Geographical – mountains, plains, deserts and coasts lead to different occupations and lifestyles

B. Cultural uniformity (unity)

  1. Geographical unity – natural boundaries of the Himalayas and the seas
  2. Political and constitutional unity – one Constitution, one citizenship, a common Parliament; national flag, anthem and emblem
  3. Common values – respect for elders, hospitality, tolerance, importance of family
  4. Religious and cultural links – pilgrimages to places all over India; the Ramayana and Mahabharata are known everywhere; festivals shared across communities
  5. Economic interdependence, transport, mass media, and Hindi and English as link languages
  6. Shared history – the freedom struggle; shared interests such as cinema and cricket

C. Effects on health and nursing

  • Different beliefs about the causes of illness, diet, childbirth, death and dying
  • Language barriers in communication
  • Preferences such as a female nurse for women, fasting during religious periods, dietary restrictions
  • Nursing implications – cultural competence, use of interpreters, respect for beliefs, flexible care plans and health education in the local language

D. Threats to unity and measures

  • Threats – communalism, casteism, regionalism and linguistic conflicts, and economic inequality between regions
  • Measures – education, secular and constitutional values, national integration programmes, equal development of all regions, inter-cultural exchange (e.g. youth exchange programmes), and responsible mass media

Conclusion India shows great diversity of race, language, religion, caste and customs, yet is united by geography, the Constitution, common values and shared traditions; nurses must respect this diversity to give culturally appropriate care.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the relationship between culture and socialisation.
answer_html:
Introduction Culture is the way of life of a society; socialisation is the process by which an individual learns that way of life. They are inseparable – culture provides the content, and socialisation is the process by which it is passed on. Learning one's own culture is called enculturation.

1. Culture provides the content of socialisation

  • Language, values, norms, beliefs, customs, skills and roles are what a child learns

2. Socialisation transmits culture

  • Culture survives from generation to generation only through socialisation – it is "social heredity"
  • Without socialisation, culture would die with each generation

3. Agencies transmit culture

  • Family – mother tongue, food habits, religion, manners
  • School – knowledge, discipline, national values
  • Peer group, religion, mass media and the workplace

4. Culture shapes personality

  • Different cultures produce different personality patterns
  • Margaret Mead's study of three tribes in New Guinea showed that gentle or aggressive behaviour and the roles of men and women depend largely on culture, not only on biology

5. Culture determines roles and behaviour

  • Gender roles, child-rearing practices, ideas of right and wrong, and health behaviour are learned through socialisation

6. Cultural change and re-socialisation

  • When a person moves to a new culture, he must learn new ways (acculturation); failure causes culture shock
  • Rapid social change requires adults to be re-socialised (e.g. learning to use digital services)

7. Importance in nursing

  • Professional socialisation – nursing students learn the culture of nursing – its values, ethics, uniform, discipline and caring attitude
  • Patients' health beliefs come from the culture learned in childhood; the nurse must understand them
  • Health education aims at re-socialisation – replacing harmful practices (e.g. discarding colostrum) with healthy ones

8. Culture-specific socialisation practices in India

  • Elders in the family act as teachers of customs and values
  • Life-cycle rituals – naming ceremony, first feeding of solid food (annaprashan), thread ceremony – mark stages of socialisation
  • Festivals and religious stories teach values such as respect, sharing and duty
  • Gender socialisation – girls are often trained in household work and taught to eat last, which can harm their nutrition; nurses must address such practices sensitively

Conclusion Culture and socialisation are two sides of the same process: culture is what is learned, and socialisation is how it is learned and passed on; both shape personality, roles and health behaviour.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain modernisation and its effects on health.
answer_html:
Introduction Modernisation is the process of social change from a traditional, rural and agricultural society to a modern, urban and industrial society, marked by the use of science and technology, rational thinking and new values. In India it was studied by Yogendra Singh ("Modernization of Indian Tradition").

1. Characteristics

  • Scientific and rational outlook
  • Industrialisation and urbanisation
  • Spread of education, mass media and communication
  • Democracy and secularism
  • Achieved status replaces ascribed status
  • Nuclear families and individualism
  • Changing role and status of women

2. Positive effects on health

  • Modern medicine – hospitals, vaccines, antibiotics → fall in death rates and rise in life expectancy
  • Better sanitation, safe water and nutrition; greater health awareness
  • Education of women → lower infant and maternal mortality, more institutional deliveries, family planning
  • Transport and communication – emergency ambulance services, telemedicine, digital health records
  • Decline of harmful practices – child marriage, superstition

3. Negative effects on health

  • Lifestyle (non-communicable) diseases – diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, obesity and cancer, due to sedentary life, junk food, stress, tobacco and alcohol
  • Mental health problems – stress, loneliness, depression and substance use
  • Breakdown of joint families → neglect of the elderly and less support in illness
  • Pollution, road accidents and occupational hazards
  • Urban slums and overcrowding → TB and other infections
  • Commercialisation of health care and inequality in access
  • Excessive screen time and mobile addiction

4. Role of the nurse

  • Health education on a healthy lifestyle – diet, exercise, no tobacco or alcohol
  • Screening for non-communicable diseases in the community
  • Encourage useful traditional practices – yoga, breastfeeding, family support
  • Community mental health and care of the elderly

5. Modernisation and westernisation

  • Westernisation (M. N. Srinivas) – changes in Indian society due to British rule and contact with Western culture – dress, food habits, language, institutions
  • Modernisation – adoption of scientific, rational and universal values and technology; it is not the same as copying the West
  • A society can modernise while keeping its own cultural identity

6. Indicators of modernisation in health

  • Fall in infant and maternal mortality, rise in life expectancy
  • Most births now take place in health institutions
  • Wider use of family planning and immunisation services

Conclusion Modernisation has improved health through science, education and better services, but has also brought lifestyle diseases, stress, pollution and loss of family support; nurses must promote its benefits and reduce its harms.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: List the basic needs of a family.
answer_html:
Introduction A family must meet certain basic needs for its members to stay healthy and live well.

Basic needs of a family

  1. Food – adequate and balanced diet
  2. Shelter – safe, ventilated housing
  3. Clothing
  4. Safe water and sanitation
  5. Health care – immunisation, treatment, family planning
  6. Education of children
  7. Income and economic security
  8. Love, affection and emotional security
  9. Safety and protection
  10. Recreation and rest

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Name the forms of marriage.
answer_html:
Definition Marriage is a socially approved union of a man and a woman that regulates sexual relations, establishes a family and gives legitimacy to children.

Forms of marriage

  1. Monogamy – one husband and one wife; the legal form for most Indians
  2. Polygamy – more than one spouse:
    • Polygyny – one man, several wives
    • Polyandry – one woman, several husbands (seen earlier among some hill tribes)
  3. Group marriage – several men married to several women (rare)

Rules of mate selection

  • Endogamy – marrying within one's own group (caste)
  • Exogamy – marrying outside a group (same gotra or clan not allowed)
  • Hypergamy – woman marries a man of higher status; hypogamy – the opposite

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Describe the primary functions of the family.
answer_html:
Introduction The family is the basic unit of society and the first school of every child. MacIver and Page divided the functions of the family into essential (primary) functions, which only the family can perform well, and non-essential (secondary) functions, which other institutions share.

A. Primary (essential) functions

1. Stable satisfaction of sex needs

  • Marriage and family provide a socially approved, regulated outlet for sex needs

2. Procreation and continuation of the race

  • The family produces children and continues the human race and the family line
  • Gives children legitimacy and identity

3. Provision of a home

  • A place of rest, security, comfort and love for all members

4. Upbringing and socialisation of children

  • The family nurtures, protects and trains children
  • Teaches language, habits, manners, values, religion and culture
  • The child's personality is largely formed in the family

5. Emotional security and affection

  • Love, care and companionship for all members, including the sick and elderly

B. Secondary (non-essential) functions

  • Economic – earning, producing and managing income and property
  • Educational – early informal education
  • Religious – transmitting faith and rituals
  • Recreational – festivals, games, outings
  • Protective – care of children, elderly, disabled and sick members
  • Health – nutrition, hygiene, home nursing, decisions about treatment
  • Social status – the family gives status (caste, class) to its members
  • Social control – disciplines members

C. Changes in modern times

  • Many secondary functions have passed to schools, hospitals, the market and the state
  • Nuclear families and working parents have reduced time for child care and care of the elderly

Nursing importance

  • The family is the unit of care in community health nursing – home visits involve the whole family
  • Family members are partners in patient care and rehabilitation

Conclusion The family's primary functions – regulation of sex, reproduction, home, upbringing of children and emotional security – make it the foundation of society and of health.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Describe the legislation related to marriage and family in India.
answer_html:
Introduction To protect women and children and to remove harmful customs, the Government of India has passed several laws on marriage and family. Nurses should know them because they deal with marriage age, dowry, violence and the rights of women.

1. Hindu Marriage Act, 1955

  • Applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs
  • Makes monogamy compulsory; bigamy is an offence
  • Minimum age: 21 years for the groom, 18 years for the bride
  • Provides for judicial separation and divorce

2. Special Marriage Act, 1954

  • Allows civil marriage between persons of any religion or caste without conversion
  • Registered before a marriage officer

3. Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006

  • Replaced the Child Marriage Restraint Act (Sarda Act), 1929
  • Child marriage is an offence; child marriages are voidable at the option of the child
  • Child Marriage Prohibition Officers are appointed

4. Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

  • Giving, taking or demanding dowry is a punishable offence

5. Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

  • Protects women from physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse at home
  • Provides protection orders, residence rights and maintenance through Protection Officers

6. Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (amended 2005)

  • Gives daughters equal rights with sons in ancestral property

7. Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956

  • Rules for adoption and maintenance of wife, children and aged parents

8. Other laws

  • Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 – makes instant triple talaq void and an offence
  • Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872 and Divorce Act, 1869
  • Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
  • Family Courts Act, 1984 – speedy settlement of family disputes
  • Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 (amended 2021) and PCPNDT Act, 1994 – prevent sex-selective abortion

Nursing importance

  • Educate families about the legal age of marriage and the dangers of early pregnancy
  • Identify and support victims of dowry harassment and domestic violence; inform them about help-lines and Protection Officers
  • Never take part in sex determination of the foetus

Conclusion Indian marriage and family laws enforce monogamy and a minimum marriage age, prohibit dowry and child marriage, protect women from violence and give daughters equal property rights.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define family. Explain the types of family and the influence of family on health. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • MacIver and Page: family is "a group defined by a sex relationship sufficiently precise and enduring to provide for the procreation and upbringing of children"
  • Burgess and Locke: "a group of persons united by ties of marriage, blood or adoption, constituting a single household, interacting with each other in their respective social roles"
  • In simple words, the family is the basic social unit of people related by marriage, blood or adoption who usually live together and care for one another

Characteristics: universal, based on emotion and affection, limited size, formative influence on members, central place in social structure, responsibility of members, regulated by social norms.

(b) Types of family (4 marks)

1. On the basis of structure (size)

  • Nuclear family – husband, wife and their unmarried children; small; common in cities
  • Joint family – two or more generations living together, sharing a common kitchen, property and worship; head is usually the eldest male (Karta); traditional in India
  • Extended family – nuclear family plus other relatives such as grandparents, uncles, aunts

2. On the basis of marriage

  • Monogamous family – one husband, one wife
  • Polygamous family – polygynous (one husband, several wives) or polyandrous (one wife, several husbands)

3. On the basis of authority

  • Patriarchal – father or eldest male is the head; most Indian families
  • Matriarchal – mother is the head (e.g. Khasi of Meghalaya)

4. On the basis of descent (lineage)

  • Patrilineal – descent and property through the father
  • Matrilineal – descent and property through the mother (Khasi, traditional Nair families of Kerala)

5. On the basis of residence after marriage

  • Patrilocal – the wife lives in the husband's home (common in India)
  • Matrilocal – the husband lives in the wife's home
  • Neolocal – the couple set up a new home

6. On the basis of relationship

  • Family of orientation – the family into which a person is born
  • Family of procreation – the family a person forms after marriage
  • Conjugal (based on marriage) and consanguineous (based on blood) families

7. Other modern forms: single-parent families, childless couples, reconstituted (step) families.

(c) Influence of family on health (4 marks)

  1. Heredity – genetic diseases (thalassaemia, haemophilia) and tendencies to diabetes, hypertension and mental illness pass through families; consanguineous marriages increase the risk
  2. Health habits – food habits, hygiene, exercise, smoking and alcohol use are learnt in the family
  3. Nutrition – the family decides what is cooked and how food is shared; girls and women may get less food in some families
  4. Family size and spacing – large families with short birth intervals have more malnutrition, anaemia and child deaths
  5. Family income – decides housing, diet, education and access to health care
  6. Care of the sick – the family gives home nursing, takes the patient to hospital, stays with him and pays for treatment
  7. Decision-making – often the elders or the husband decide about treatment, delivery place and family planning
  8. Emotional support – a caring family speeds recovery and protects mental health; family conflict, divorce, alcoholism or violence cause stress and illness
  9. Socialisation of children – healthy habits, immunisation and education of children depend on parents
  10. Care of the elderly and disabled – joint families give security; nuclear families may leave the elderly lonely

Role of the nurse

  • Use the family as the unit of care in community health nursing
  • Assess family structure, resources, health practices and decision-makers
  • Health education on nutrition, hygiene, family planning and immunisation
  • Involve the family in care and rehabilitation; support caregivers
  • Identify family problems – violence, addiction, neglect – and refer

Conclusion The family is the basic unit of society and can be nuclear, joint or extended, patriarchal or matriarchal, patrilineal or matrilineal. Through heredity, habits, income, decisions and emotional support it strongly influences the health of its members, which is why nurses work with the family as a whole.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What is the family life cycle?
answer_html:
Definition The family life cycle is the series of stages through which a family passes from its formation at marriage to its end at the death of the spouses. Each stage has its own developmental tasks and health needs.

Evelyn Duvall's eight stages

  1. Married couple without children
