  2. Childbearing family – oldest child up to 30 months
  3. Family with preschool children
  4. Family with school-age children
  5. Family with teenagers
  6. Launching family – children leave home
  7. Middle-aged parents – "empty nest" to retirement
  8. Ageing family – retirement to death of both spouses

Importance: helps the nurse anticipate needs at each stage – family planning, immunisation, adolescent counselling, care of the elderly.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define endogamy and exogamy.
answer_html:
Endogamy

  • A rule that requires a person to marry within his own group – caste, sub-caste, religion, tribe or class
  • Example: caste endogamy in India

Exogamy

  • A rule that requires a person to marry outside a particular group
  • Examples:
    • Gotra exogamy – marriage within the same gotra is prohibited among many Hindus
    • Sapinda exogamy – marriage between close blood relatives (within prohibited degrees) is not allowed
    • Village exogamy in parts of north India
    • Clan exogamy among tribes

Health importance: consanguineous marriages (between close relatives) increase the risk of inherited disorders such as thalassaemia and other recessive diseases – premarital counselling and screening help.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What is divorce? Give its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Divorce is the legal dissolution of a valid marriage by a court of law, after which both partners are free to remarry. In India it is governed by personal laws such as the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (including divorce by mutual consent) and the Special Marriage Act, 1954.

Causes

  1. Incompatibility and lack of understanding
  2. Cruelty and domestic violence
  3. Dowry harassment
  4. Alcoholism and drug addiction
  5. Adultery; desertion
  6. Interference of in-laws
  7. Infertility; serious mental illness
  8. Economic independence of women and changing values; urban life and individualism

Effects: emotional stress, financial problems and adjustment problems in children – families need counselling and support.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define marriage. Explain its aims and the marriage rites in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Marriage is a socially and legally approved union of a man and a woman that gives them the rights and duties of husband and wife and makes their children legitimate.

  • Westermarck: marriage is a relation of one or more men to one or more women, recognised by custom or law, involving rights and duties for both partners and for the children born of it
  • Malinowski: marriage is a contract for the production and maintenance of children

A. Aims and importance of marriage

  1. Regulation of sexual behaviour
  2. Procreation and legitimacy of children
  3. Upbringing and socialisation of children
  4. Companionship and emotional security
  5. Formation of the family and kinship ties
  6. Economic cooperation and division of labour
  7. Inheritance of property and family name
  8. Social status
  9. Religious duty – Hindu marriage aims at dharma (duty), praja (children) and rati (pleasure)

B. Marriage rites in India

  • Hindu marriage – a sacrament (samskara):
    • betrothal, kanyadaan (giving away of the bride), panigrahana (taking the bride's hand), vivaha homa (sacred fire)
    • saptapadi – the seven steps around the fire; where it is the custom, the marriage is complete with the seventh step
    • mangalsutra and sindoor
  • Muslim marriage (Nikah) – a civil contract:
    • proposal (ijab) and acceptance (qubul) in the same meeting before witnesses
    • mehr (dower) payable to the bride; performed by a Qazi; a nikahnama is recorded
  • Christian marriage:
    • announcement of banns; exchange of vows and rings before a priest and witnesses in church; registered under the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872
  • Civil (registered) marriage:
    • under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, before a Marriage Officer, after 30 days' notice; used for inter-caste and inter-religious marriages
  • Tribal forms – marriage by mutual consent or elopement, by service, by exchange, and bride price

C. Marriage and health

  • Legal age – 21 years for men and 18 years for women (Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006)
  • Early marriage leads to teenage pregnancy, anaemia and maternal deaths
  • Premarital counselling and screening (thalassaemia, sickle cell, HIV) improve family health

Conclusion Marriage is a social institution that regulates sex, legitimises children and forms the family; in India it is a sacrament for Hindus, a contract for Muslims, a sacred covenant for Christians and a civil contract under the Special Marriage Act.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the changing trends in the Indian family.
answer_html:
Introduction The traditional Indian family was joint, patriarchal, patrilineal and patrilocal. Under the influence of industrialisation, urbanisation, education, legislation and mass media, it is changing rapidly.

1. Changes in structure

  • Shift from joint to nuclear families; smaller family size
  • Rise of single-parent, dual-career and single-person (elderly living alone) households

2. Changes in authority

  • Patriarchal authority has weakened; decisions are more democratic, and women take part

3. Status of women

  • More education, employment and economic independence
  • Legal rights – equal share for daughters in ancestral property (Hindu Succession Amendment, 2005)

4. Changes in marriage

  • Later age at marriage
  • More self-chosen (love) marriages and inter-caste marriages
  • Rise in divorce and separation; acceptance of widow remarriage

5. Transfer of functions

  • Many traditional functions have moved to other institutions:
    • education → schools
    • health care → hospitals
    • recreation → mass media
    • economic production → factories and offices
    • child care → crèches and anganwadis
  • The family keeps its emotional and socialisation functions

6. Changes in relationships

  • Weakening of kinship ties; growing individualism; generation gap
  • Small family norm – fewer children (total fertility rate about 2)

7. Care of the elderly

  • Less support from children → old-age homes; the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 makes children responsible for maintaining parents

8. Causes of change

  • Industrialisation and urbanisation, migration for jobs, education, women's employment, legislation, westernisation, housing problems and economic pressures

9. Effects on health

  • Positive – more attention to each child, family planning, better health of women and children
  • Negative – loneliness and neglect of the elderly, lack of help during illness and childbirth, stress, marital conflict, children left alone, mental health problems and substance use

10. Role of the nurse

  • Family health assessment and family-centred care
  • Link families with support services – home care, day-care centres, elderly care
  • Counselling and strengthening family ties

Conclusion The Indian family is changing from a large, joint, patriarchal unit to a small, nuclear, more equal one that has handed over many functions to other institutions; these changes bring both health benefits and new problems that nurses must address.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define social stratification.
answer_html:
Definition Social stratification is the division of society into layers (strata) arranged in a hierarchy of higher and lower positions, based on wealth, power, prestige, birth or occupation.

Ogburn and Nimkoff: the process by which individuals and groups are ranked in a more or less enduring hierarchy of status.

Characteristics

  1. Social – created by society, not by nature
  2. Universal – found in all societies
  3. Ancient
  4. Takes different forms
  5. Affects life chances – health, education, income

Forms: caste, class, estate and slavery.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: List the characteristics of the caste system.
answer_html:
Introduction Caste is a closed system of stratification based on birth. G. S. Ghurye described its main features:

  1. Segmental division of society – each caste is a distinct group with its own rules
  2. Hierarchy – castes are ranked from high to low
  3. Restrictions on food and social intercourse – rules about who can eat with whom
  4. Civil and religious disabilities and privileges – some castes were denied access to temples, wells and schools (untouchability)
  5. Restricted choice of occupation – hereditary occupations
  6. Endogamy – marriage only within one's own caste

Membership is by birth and cannot normally be changed.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Differentiate between caste and class.
answer_html:
Introduction Caste and class are two forms of social stratification.

Caste Class
based on birth based on wealth, education, occupation
closed system – membership cannot be changed open system – people can move up or down
endogamy is compulsory no strict rule of marriage
hereditary occupation free choice of occupation
social mobility is very limited social mobility is common
religious sanction no religious basis
found mainly in India found in all societies

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain social mobility with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Social mobility means the movement of individuals or groups from one social position (status) to another. P. A. Sorokin, who studied it in detail, described it as any transition of an individual or social object from one social position to another. It is common in an open (class) system and rare in a closed (caste) system.

Types of social mobility

1. Horizontal mobility

  • Change of position at the same level – no rise or fall in status
  • Example: a staff nurse moves from a district hospital to another hospital as a staff nurse; a teacher changes schools

2. Vertical mobility – change in rank

  • Upward mobility – rise in status
    • Example: a staff nurse promoted to nursing superintendent; a labourer's son becoming a doctor
  • Downward mobility – fall in status
    • Example: a businessman becoming bankrupt; an officer demoted

3. Intergenerational mobility

  • Change in status between generations – children reach a different status from their parents
  • Example: the daughter of an illiterate farmer becomes a nursing tutor

4. Intragenerational mobility

  • Change in status within one person's lifetime (career mobility)
  • Example: a nursing student becomes a staff nurse, then a nursing officer

5. Structural mobility

  • Mobility caused by changes in the economy or society (new jobs created by the IT industry)

Factors that promote social mobility

  • Education – the most powerful factor
  • Occupation, income and skill
  • Industrialisation and urbanisation
  • Migration
  • Legislation and reservation policies
  • Marriage (hypergamy)
  • Individual ambition and hard work

Factors that limit mobility

  • Caste rigidity, poverty, illiteracy, gender discrimination, lack of opportunities

Effects

  • Positive: reward for merit, motivation, weakening of caste barriers
  • Negative: stress, insecurity, breakdown of traditional ties

Nursing relevance

  • Nursing offers upward mobility to many young women and men from rural and poor families
  • Education and training in nursing change both individual and family status

Conclusion Social mobility may be horizontal or vertical, intergenerational or intragenerational; education and economic development are the main forces promoting it in modern India.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the influence of class, caste and race on health.
answer_html:
Introduction Social stratification decides how much wealth, power, education and access to services a person has. These, in turn, affect health. Health indicators in India differ widely between the rich and poor, upper and lower castes, and among different racial and ethnic groups.

A. Influence of class (socio-economic status)

  • Low-income groups have poor housing, overcrowding, unsafe water and poor sanitation → more TB, diarrhoea, worm infestations
  • Malnutrition and anaemia are more common among the poor
  • Less education → less awareness of health and delayed treatment
  • Cannot afford private care; depend on government services; out-of-pocket spending pushes families into poverty
  • Occupational hazards in unskilled jobs
  • Higher classes suffer more lifestyle diseases – obesity, diabetes, heart disease – due to rich diet and inactivity

B. Influence of caste

  • Historically lower castes were denied education, land and services – these disadvantages still affect income and health
  • Occupational diseases – manual scavenging and sewer work cause infections, injuries and deaths (manual scavenging is now banned)
  • Discrimination in access to water sources, schools and sometimes health services in some areas
  • Endogamy and consanguineous marriage within small caste groups increase genetic disorders
  • Caste-based food habits influence nutrition
  • Government programmes and reservations aim to reduce these gaps

C. Influence of race

  • Race refers to groups with common inherited physical features (skin colour, hair, facial features)
  • Genetic diseases are more common in some groups:
    • Sickle cell disease – many tribal groups of central and western India and people of African origin
    • Thalassaemia – higher in some communities (Sindhis, Punjabis, Gujaratis, Bengalis)
    • Skin cancer – more in fair-skinned people; vitamin D deficiency more in dark-skinned people living away from the sun
  • Racial and ethnic discrimination causes stress and poor access to care in many countries

D. Role of the nurse

  • Give equal, respectful care to all patients regardless of caste, class or race
  • Identify vulnerable groups and link them to schemes such as Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY), Janani Suraksha Yojana and nutrition programmes
  • Screen high-risk groups for genetic diseases (sickle cell, thalassaemia)
  • Health education suited to the literacy level of the community

Conclusion Class, caste and race influence income, education, living conditions, occupation and genetics, and through these they decide a person's health; nurses must work for equal access to care.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define social stratification. Explain caste as a form of social stratification and the present trend of the caste system in modern India. (2 + 4 + 4)
answer_html:
(a) Social stratification (2 marks) Definition

  • Social stratification is the arrangement of individuals and groups in a hierarchy of higher and lower layers (strata) on the basis of birth, wealth, power, prestige or occupation
  • Ogburn and Nimkoff: it is the process by which individuals and groups are ranked in a more or less enduring hierarchy of status

Characteristics

  • It is social (made by society), universal, ancient, found in different forms, and consequential – it affects life chances such as education, health and income

Forms: caste, class, estate and slavery.

(b) Caste as a form of social stratification (4 marks) 1. Definition

  • Caste is a hereditary, endogamous social group in which membership is fixed by birth, with a traditional occupation and a fixed position in a hierarchy
  • S. V. Ketkar: a caste is a social group with two characteristics – membership is confined to those born into it, and members are forbidden to marry outside the group

2. Origin of caste – theories

  • Traditional (religious) theory – the four varnas (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) arose from different parts of the creator (Rig Veda)
  • Racial theory (Risley) – arose from contact between invading groups and local people
  • Occupational theory (Nesfield) – caste developed from hereditary occupations
  • Political theory – created to preserve the dominance of certain groups
  • Most scholars believe caste developed gradually from many causes

3. Features of caste (G. S. Ghurye)

  1. Segmental division of society
  2. Hierarchy – castes ranked one above the other
  3. Restrictions on feeding and social intercourse
  4. Civil and religious disabilities and privileges – practice of untouchability in the past
  5. Lack of free choice of occupation
  6. Restrictions on marriage – endogamy

4. Positive aspects (functions)

  • Social security and support to members
  • Division of labour and transmission of skills
  • Preservation of culture and traditions
  • Social control over behaviour

5. Negative aspects

  • Untouchability and discrimination
  • Inequality and exploitation of lower castes
  • Barrier to social mobility and national unity
  • Caste conflicts, honour killings
  • Restriction of inter-caste marriage and of free choice of occupation

(c) Present trend of the caste system in modern India (4 marks) 1. Constitutional and legal changes

  • The Constitution guarantees equality (Article 14), prohibits discrimination on the basis of caste (Article 15) and abolishes untouchability (Article 17)
  • Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
  • Reservation in education, government jobs and legislatures for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes

2. Weakening of traditional features

  • Occupational restrictions have weakened – people choose occupations by education and opportunity
  • Restrictions on food and social contact have nearly disappeared in cities – people eat together in hotels, offices, hostels and hospitals
  • Untouchability is legally abolished and has greatly reduced, though not fully eliminated
  • Inter-caste marriages are increasing, especially in urban educated families

3. Factors responsible for change

  • Education, urbanisation and industrialisation
  • Modern transport and communication
  • Democracy and adult franchise
  • Social reform movements (Phule, Ambedkar, Gandhi)
  • Sanskritisation (M. N. Srinivas) – lower castes adopting customs of higher castes to raise their status
  • Westernisation and modern values of equality

4. Areas where caste still persists

  • Marriage – endogamy is still largely followed (matrimonial advertisements by caste)
  • Politics – caste is used for mobilising votes ("vote banks"); caste associations have become pressure groups
  • Rural areas – discrimination in some places
  • Caste identity has become a basis for demanding rights and benefits

5. Overall trend

  • Caste has changed from a ritual hierarchy to a political and social identity; its rigid features are weakening, but it remains important in marriage and politics

Nursing relevance

  • Nurses must give equal care to all patients without caste discrimination – it is both an ethical duty and a legal one
  • Understanding caste helps in community work, where caste may affect participation and access to services

Conclusion Social stratification ranks people in a hierarchy; caste is its closed, birth-based form with endogamy, hierarchy and occupational restrictions. In modern India, laws, education, urbanisation and democracy have weakened caste practices, though caste still survives in marriage and politics.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Differentiate between ascribed and achieved status.
answer_html:
Introduction Status is the position of a person in a group or society, with its rights and duties. Ralph Linton divided it into ascribed and achieved status.

Ascribed status Achieved status
given at birth or assigned without effort earned by one's own effort, ability and choice
based on age, sex, caste, race, family based on education, occupation, skill, income
fixed; difficult to change can change – allows social mobility
common in traditional (closed) societies common in modern (open) societies
e.g. son, daughter, prince, member of a caste e.g. nurse, doctor, teacher, elected leader

Note: role is the expected behaviour attached to a status – the dynamic side of status.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define race. Name the major racial groups in India.
answer_html:
Definition Race is a large group of people who share certain inherited physical features – skin colour, hair, eye shape, nose form, head shape and stature – that distinguish them from other groups. Modern genetics shows that all humans belong to one species, and that differences within a race are greater than those between races.

Racial groups in India (B. S. Guha)

  1. Negrito – e.g. Onge and Jarawa of the Andaman Islands
  2. Proto-Australoid – e.g. many central Indian tribes such as Bhil, Santhal and Munda
  3. Mongoloid – north-east India and the Himalayan region
  4. Mediterranean – the most widespread group
  5. Western Brachycephals (Alpine, Dinaric, Armenoid)
  6. Nordic – north-west India

Applied: certain inherited disorders are commoner in some communities (e.g. sickle cell disease among some tribal groups of central India); the Constitution forbids discrimination by race (Article 15).

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the functions and dysfunctions of social stratification.
answer_html:
Introduction Social stratification is the division of society into layers (strata) that are ranked one above the other on the basis of wealth, power and prestige. It is found in all societies. The functionalist view (Davis and Moore) says stratification is useful to society, while the conflict view (Karl Marx, Melvin Tumin) points out its harmful effects.

A. Functions

  1. Fills important positions – higher rewards (income, prestige) attract the most able and qualified people to the most important jobs (e.g. doctors, scientists)
  2. Motivation – people work hard and compete to rise
  3. Division of labour and specialisation – everyone has a definite place, rights and duties, giving social order
  4. Social identity – status gives people a sense of who they are
  5. Stability and security – in the traditional caste system, occupation and social support were assured
  6. Social control – each stratum has its norms, which regulate behaviour

B. Dysfunctions

  1. Inequality in life chances – unequal access to education, health care and income; poverty passes from one generation to the next
  2. Talent is wasted – able children of poor families cannot rise; social mobility is limited, especially in a caste system
  3. Discrimination and exploitation – untouchability, social exclusion and denial of rights to lower strata
  4. Conflict and tension between groups – class struggle, caste conflicts
  5. Low self-esteem and frustration among the lower strata, which may lead to deviance
  6. Unequal political power and concentration of resources in a few hands

C. Effects on health

  • Lower strata suffer more malnutrition, infections, infant and maternal deaths and have poorer access to care
  • Higher strata are more prone to lifestyle diseases

D. Measures to reduce harmful effects

  • Constitutional safeguards – equality before law (Article 14), no discrimination (Article 15), abolition of untouchability (Article 17), promotion of the interests of weaker sections (Article 46)
  • Reservation, scholarships and welfare schemes
  • Free health services and health insurance for the poor

E. Role of the nurse

  • Give equal, respectful care to all patients regardless of caste or class
  • Give priority to vulnerable groups and link them with welfare schemes

Conclusion Stratification helps society fill important positions, motivates people and maintains order, but it also creates inequality, wastes talent, causes discrimination and conflict, and damages the health of the lower strata.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain social class and its measurement (socio-economic status scales).
answer_html:
Introduction A social class is a group of people who share a similar position in society, based mainly on wealth, income, occupation and education. MacIver and Page: "a social class is any portion of a community marked off from the rest by social status." Unlike caste, class is open – a person can move up or down.

1. Characteristics

  • Open – social mobility is possible
  • Achieved – based on one's own effort
  • Based mainly on economic factors
  • Class consciousness – members feel they belong together
  • Similar lifestyle within a class
  • Arranged in a hierarchy; no religious sanction

2. Classification

  • Upper, middle and lower classes, each with sub-divisions
  • Karl Marx – the owners of the means of production (bourgeoisie) and the workers (proletariat)

3. Determinants of class

  • Income and wealth, occupation, education, housing and residence, family background, lifestyle and power

4. Measurement – socio-economic status (SES) scales used in India

a. Kuppuswamy scale (mainly urban)

  • Based on three items:
    • education of the head of the family
    • occupation of the head of the family
    • total monthly family income
  • Total score (3–29) classifies families as upper, upper middle, lower middle, upper lower and lower
  • Income ranges are updated regularly using the consumer price index

b. B. G. Prasad scale (urban and rural)

  • Based on per capita monthly income
  • Five classes, from I (upper) to V (lower); also updated with the price index

c. Udai Pareek scale (rural)

  • Considers caste, occupation, education, land, house, farm power, material possessions, social participation and family

5. Importance in health and nursing

  • SES is a strong determinant of health – affects nutrition, housing, sanitation, disease and use of health services
  • Used in community health surveys and research
  • Helps identify families needing help and plan welfare programmes
  • Eligibility for schemes such as free treatment and health insurance for the poor depends on economic status

6. Role of the nurse

  • Assess SES during family health assessment
  • Plan affordable care and link poor families to welfare and insurance schemes

Conclusion Social class is an open, achieved ranking based mainly on economic factors; in India it is measured by scales such as Kuppuswamy, B. G. Prasad and Udai Pareek, which help nurses identify needy families and plan care.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define social disorganisation.
answer_html:
Definition Social disorganisation is a condition in which the relationships, rules and institutions of a society break down, so that society can no longer control the behaviour of its members effectively.

Elliott and Merrill: it is the process by which the relationships between members of a group are broken or dissolved.

Causes

  1. Rapid social change and cultural lag
  2. Conflict of values between old and new generations
  3. Urbanisation, migration and industrialisation
  4. Wars, riots and natural disasters
  5. Poverty and unemployment

Forms / examples: personal disorganisation (suicide, addiction), family disorganisation (divorce, desertion, domestic violence) and community disorganisation (crime, corruption, communal riots).

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What are social norms?
answer_html:
Definition Norms are the shared rules or standards of behaviour that a group expects its members to follow in particular situations. They tell people what they should and should not do.

Types of norms

  1. Folkways – everyday customs and manners (greeting elders, table manners); breaking them brings mild disapproval
  2. Mores – norms with moral importance (honesty, not stealing, caring for parents); breaking them brings strong disapproval
  3. Customs and traditions – long-established practices
  4. Laws – formal norms made and enforced by the state
  5. Taboos – strong prohibitions

Functions: guide behaviour, maintain order, give predictability, act as a means of social control.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: List the types of social systems.
answer_html:
Definition A social system is a group of interacting individuals whose relationships are organised by shared norms, roles and status (Talcott Parsons).

Types of social systems (Parsons)

  1. Universalistic–achievement – status by merit, rules apply to all (modern industrial society, e.g. USA)
  2. Universalistic–ascription – common rules, but status by birth or group membership
  3. Particularistic–achievement – status by merit within close relationships (traditional China)
  4. Particularistic–ascription – status by birth and kinship (traditional caste society)

Sub-systems of society: family, economic, political, religious, educational and health systems.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define social control and name its means.
answer_html:
Definition Social control is the process by which society regulates the behaviour of its members so that they follow its norms and values, maintaining order and stability.

Means of social control

  1. Informal means
    • Folkways, mores and customs
    • Religion and morality
    • Family and peer group
    • Public opinion, praise, ridicule, gossip
  2. Formal means
    • Law and the courts
    • Police and administration
    • Education
    • Rules of institutions (hospital rules, codes of conduct)

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the fundamental rights of the individual.
answer_html:
Introduction Fundamental rights are the basic rights guaranteed to every citizen by Part III of the Constitution of India (Articles 12–35). They protect the dignity, freedom and equality of individuals, and can be enforced in the courts.

The six fundamental rights

1. Right to equality (Articles 14–18)

  • Equality before law and equal protection of laws (Art. 14)
  • No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Art. 15)
  • Equality of opportunity in public employment (Art. 16)
  • Abolition of untouchability (Art. 17)
  • Abolition of titles (Art. 18)

2. Right to freedom (Articles 19–22)

  • Six freedoms (Art. 19): speech and expression; peaceful assembly; forming associations; moving freely; residing anywhere in India; practising any profession or occupation
  • Protection in respect of conviction for offences (Art. 20)
  • Protection of life and personal liberty (Art. 21) – the courts have interpreted this to include the right to health, dignity, privacy, emergency medical care and a clean environment
  • Right to education (Art. 21A) – free and compulsory education for children of 6–14 years
  • Protection against arbitrary arrest and detention (Art. 22)

3. Right against exploitation (Articles 23–24)

  • Prohibits trafficking in human beings and forced labour (Art. 23)
  • Prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines and hazardous work (Art. 24)

4. Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25–28)

  • Freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion

5. Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29–30)

  • Protection of the language, script and culture of minorities; right of minorities to establish educational institutions

6. Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32)

  • Right to approach the Supreme Court (and High Courts) to enforce fundamental rights through writs – habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto
  • Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called it the "heart and soul" of the Constitution

(The right to property is no longer a fundamental right; it is now a legal right.)

Nursing importance

  • Every patient has a right to life, dignity, privacy and equal treatment without discrimination
  • Emergency care must not be refused
  • Nurses must respect consent and confidentiality and protect children from labour and abuse

Conclusion The six fundamental rights – equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights and constitutional remedies – protect every citizen and form the legal base of patients' rights.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the root causes of population growth in India.
answer_html:
Introduction India has become the most populous country in the world. Its population was about 121 crore in the 2011 Census, and it has continued to grow. Rapid population growth puts pressure on food, housing, health services, employment and the environment. The total fertility rate has fallen to about 2.0 (NFHS-5, 2019–21), but because a large proportion of the population is young, numbers will keep rising for some decades.

Root causes of population growth

1. Fall in death rate with a slower fall in birth rate

  • Better medical care, vaccines, antibiotics, control of epidemics and famines have reduced deaths
  • Birth rate fell much more slowly – this gap (demographic transition) caused rapid growth

2. Early marriage

  • Marriage at a young age lengthens the reproductive period and leads to more children

3. Illiteracy, especially of women

  • Uneducated women marry early, know less about contraception and have less say in family size

4. Poverty

  • Children are seen as extra earning hands and as security in old age
  • High infant mortality in the past made parents have more children "to be safe"

5. Son preference

  • Couples keep having children until they have a son

6. Religious and cultural beliefs

  • Some consider children a gift of God and oppose contraception
  • Social pressure to prove fertility early after marriage

7. Low use of contraceptives

  • Lack of awareness, fear of side effects, poor access in remote areas
  • Unmet need for family planning

8. Joint family system

  • Costs of child rearing are shared, so couples feel less burden

9. Other factors

  • Lack of recreation, migration from neighbouring countries, and in the past, polygamy

Effects (in brief)

  • Unemployment, poverty, overcrowding, slums, pollution, shortage of food and water, pressure on schools and hospitals

Measures

  • Family planning services under the National Family Planning Programme; a wider choice of contraceptives (injectable Antara, weekly pill Chhaya)
  • Female education and raising the age of marriage
  • Improving child survival so parents feel secure with fewer children
  • Mass media and health education; incentives; Mission Parivar Vikas in high-fertility districts

Nursing role: counselling couples, providing contraceptive services, promoting spacing of births and the two-child norm, educating adolescents.

Conclusion Population growth in India results from falling death rates, early marriage, illiteracy, poverty, son preference and low contraceptive use; education of women and family planning are the key remedies.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain poverty as a social problem.
answer_html:
Introduction Poverty is a condition in which a person or family lacks the income and resources to meet basic needs – food, clothing, shelter, health care and education. It is both a cause and an effect of ill health.

1. Types

  • Absolute poverty – inability to meet the minimum needs for survival; measured by a poverty line
  • Relative poverty – being poor compared with others in the same society
  • Multidimensional poverty – deprivation in health, education and living standards (nutrition, schooling, sanitation, housing)

2. Causes

  • Population growth
  • Unemployment and underemployment
  • Illiteracy and lack of skills
  • Dependence on agriculture, small landholdings, crop failure
  • Inequality – caste, gender and regional
  • Illness – catastrophic health expenditure pushes families into debt
  • Social customs – heavy spending on weddings, dowry
  • Addictions – alcohol and gambling
  • Natural disasters

3. Effects

  • Malnutrition, anaemia and stunting
  • Communicable diseases – TB, diarrhoea, worm infestations
  • High infant and maternal mortality
  • Child labour, school dropout
  • Crime, prostitution, beggary
  • Poor housing, slums
  • Stress and mental illness

4. Measures to reduce poverty

  • MGNREGA – guaranteed rural employment
  • Public Distribution System and the National Food Security Act, 2013
  • Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – housing
  • Ayushman Bharat – PM-JAY – health insurance for poor families
  • National Rural and Urban Livelihood Missions – self-help groups
  • Skill development, free education, mid-day meals, old-age pensions

5. Role of the nurse

  • Identify poor and vulnerable families during home visits
  • Guide them to free services and government schemes
  • Health education on low-cost nutritious food
  • Prioritise them for immunisation, antenatal care and nutrition programmes

Measurement of poverty

  • Poverty line – the minimum income or consumption needed for basic needs; people below it are "below poverty line" (BPL)
  • Multidimensional Poverty Index (NITI Aayog) – measures deprivation in health (nutrition, child and adolescent mortality, maternal health), education (years of schooling, school attendance) and standard of living (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account)

Vicious cycle of poverty and ill health

  • Poverty → poor food, housing and sanitation → illness → loss of wages and cost of treatment → deeper poverty

Conclusion Poverty, caused by unemployment, illiteracy, population growth and inequality, leads to malnutrition, disease and social problems; government schemes and community nursing help break the cycle of poverty and ill health.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Write a short note on child labour and child abuse.
answer_html:
Introduction Children are the most vulnerable members of society. Child labour and child abuse deprive children of their health, education and childhood, and both are prohibited by Indian law.

A. Child labour 1. Definition: employment of children in work that harms their health, education and development. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act (1986, amended 2016) prohibits employment of children below 14 years in any occupation (except helping in family enterprises after school hours) and of adolescents (14–18 years) in hazardous work. Article 24 of the Constitution also prohibits it.

2. Causes

  • Poverty and debt
  • Illiteracy of parents
  • Large family size
  • Demand for cheap labour
  • Migration, orphanhood

3. Effects on health

  • Malnutrition, stunted growth
  • Injuries, exposure to chemicals, dust and heat
  • Respiratory and skin diseases
  • Loss of education, exploitation, abuse

B. Child abuse 1. Definition: any act or neglect by an adult that causes physical or emotional harm to a child.

2. Types

  • Physical abuse – beating, burns, injuries
  • Emotional abuse – humiliation, threats, rejection
  • Sexual abuse – covered by the POCSO Act, 2012 (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences)
  • Neglect – failure to provide food, care, schooling or medical care

3. Warning signs for nurses

  • Unexplained or repeated injuries, injuries in different stages of healing
  • Fearful, withdrawn behaviour; regression
  • Malnutrition, poor hygiene, delayed treatment

C. Measures

  • Strict enforcement of child labour and POCSO laws; Juvenile Justice Act, 2015
  • Right to Education (6–14 years) and mid-day meals keep children in school
  • CHILDLINE 1098 – emergency helpline
  • Rehabilitation of rescued children; support to poor families

D. Role of the nurse

  • Identify and report suspected abuse (reporting is mandatory under POCSO)
  • Give sensitive, child-friendly care; preserve evidence; maintain confidentiality
  • Health education of parents on positive parenting
  • Refer to child welfare committees and counselling services

Conclusion Child labour and child abuse are serious social problems that harm children's health and future; laws, education and alert health workers are essential to prevent them.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Describe the social welfare programmes in India.
answer_html:
Introduction Social welfare programmes are organised services provided by the government (and voluntary agencies) to help weaker and vulnerable sections – women, children, the elderly, the disabled and the poor – to live with dignity. India, as a welfare state, runs many such programmes.

1. Programmes for children

  • Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) – since 1975; supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health check-up, pre-school education through Anganwadi centres
  • PM POSHAN (mid-day meal) in schools
  • Mission Vatsalya – child protection services; CHILDLINE 1098
  • Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram – screening of children for defects and diseases

2. Programmes for women

  • Janani Suraksha Yojana – cash incentive for institutional delivery
  • Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana – maternity benefit
  • Beti Bachao Beti Padhao – to improve the child sex ratio and girls' education
  • One Stop Centres (Sakhi) and women's helpline 181 for women facing violence
  • Self-help groups for economic empowerment

3. Programmes for the elderly

  • National Social Assistance Programme – old-age, widow and disability pensions
  • National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly
  • Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007

4. Programmes for persons with disabilities

  • Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 – reservation, education, accessibility
  • Accessible India Campaign, aids and appliances (ADIP scheme)

5. Programmes for the poor

  • MGNREGA – 100 days of guaranteed wage employment
  • National Food Security Act and Public Distribution System
  • Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – housing
  • Ayushman Bharat – PM-JAY – health insurance cover for poor families
  • Swachh Bharat Mission – toilets and sanitation

6. Programmes for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes

  • Scholarships, hostels, reservation, special development programmes

Role of the nurse

  • Know these schemes and guide eligible patients and families to use them
  • Work with Anganwadi workers, ASHAs and social workers
  • Help with registration, documentation and referral
  • Identify beneficiaries during community visits

Conclusion India's social welfare programmes support children, women, the elderly, the disabled and the poor in nutrition, health, income and protection; nurses act as a bridge between these schemes and the people.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Discuss prostitution under the headings: types, causes and measures for prevention. (2 + 5 + 3)
answer_html:
Introduction Prostitution is one of the oldest social problems. It is the sexual exploitation of persons for commercial purposes, in which sexual services are exchanged for money or other benefits. In India, the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 deals with it. Many women and children in prostitution are victims of trafficking, poverty and deception rather than free choice. It is closely linked with sexually transmitted infections, HIV/AIDS and exploitation.

(a) Types of prostitution (2 marks)

  1. Brothel-based – women live and work in a brothel controlled by a brothel-keeper
  2. Street-based – soliciting in public places
  3. Call girls and escort services – arranged by telephone, agents or online
  4. Hotel, lodge and highway-based – along transport routes, catering to drivers and migrant workers
  5. Traditional or religious – customs such as the Devadasi system, in which girls were dedicated to temples and later exploited; now banned by state laws
  6. Clandestine or part-time – women who do it secretly alongside other work
  7. Child prostitution – the most serious form; always a crime and a form of child sexual abuse
  8. Male and transgender sex work

(b) Causes of prostitution (5 marks)

1. Economic causes

  • Poverty and the need to feed the family
  • Unemployment and lack of skills
  • Low wages and economic dependence of women
  • Debt

2. Social causes

  • Family disorganisation – broken homes, desertion, divorce, widowhood without support
  • Child marriage, unhappy marriage, dowry harassment
  • Social stigma that prevents rehabilitated women from returning home
  • Gender discrimination and low status of women
  • Illiteracy

3. Trafficking and deception

  • Kidnapping and luring of girls with false promises of jobs or marriage
  • Organised trafficking networks from poor villages and neighbouring countries
  • Sale of girls by relatives

4. Cultural and religious causes

  • Traditional practices such as the Devadasi system in some regions
  • Some communities where it became a hereditary occupation

5. Psychological causes

  • Childhood neglect and lack of affection
  • Low self-esteem, emotional insecurity
  • Desire for an easy or luxurious life

6. Urbanisation and migration

  • Large numbers of single migrant men in cities create demand
  • Weak social control in cities

7. Other causes

  • Drug addiction
  • Lack of rehabilitation and support services
  • Corruption and weak enforcement of laws
  • Influence of pornography and media

(c) Measures for prevention (3 marks)

1. Legal measures

  • Strict enforcement of the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, which punishes brothel-keeping, pimping, procuring and trafficking
  • Trafficking of persons is a serious offence under the criminal law (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)
  • POCSO Act, 2012 protects children
  • State laws banning the Devadasi system
  • Anti-Human Trafficking Units in police

2. Economic measures

  • Education and vocational training for girls and women
  • Employment and self-employment schemes; self-help groups
  • Poverty-reduction programmes

3. Social measures

  • Strengthening the family; preventing child marriage and dowry
  • Public awareness about trafficking and fake job offers
  • Removing stigma so that rescued women can be accepted back

4. Rescue and rehabilitation

  • Rescue, protective homes and shelter homes (Swadhar Greh)
  • Schemes for prevention of trafficking and rehabilitation of victims (Ujjawala, now part of Mission Shakti)
  • Counselling, health care, legal aid and reintegration into society

5. Health measures

  • Prevention and treatment of STIs and HIV/AIDS – targeted interventions under the National AIDS Control Programme, condom promotion, regular check-ups
  • Care of the children of women in prostitution

6. Role of voluntary organisations – NGOs play a major role in rescue, rehabilitation and awareness.

Role of the nurse

  • Provide non-judgemental, respectful and confidential care
  • STI/HIV screening, counselling and treatment; family planning services
  • Identify victims of trafficking (especially minors) and inform the authorities
  • Health education in high-risk communities
  • Refer to rehabilitation services and support groups

Conclusion Prostitution takes many forms and arises mainly from poverty, family breakdown, trafficking and gender inequality. Its prevention needs strict laws against trafficking, economic empowerment of women, social acceptance and rehabilitation of victims, along with health services to prevent HIV and other infections.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Describe the major social problems in India and the role of the nurse in reducing them. (2 + 5 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction and definition (2 marks)

  • A social problem is a condition that affects a large number of people in a harmful way and that society believes should be corrected through collective action
  • Social problems arise from social disorganisation – rapid social change, poverty, inequality and weakening of social control
  • They affect health directly (injury, disease, malnutrition) and indirectly (stress, poor access to care)

(b) Major social problems in India (5 marks)

1. Poverty and unemployment

  • Lack of income for basic needs; leads to malnutrition, disease, child labour and crime

2. Population explosion

  • Pressure on food, housing, jobs and health services

3. Illiteracy

  • Especially among women; leads to early marriage, large families and poor health awareness

4. Housing problems and slums

  • Overcrowding, poor ventilation, no sanitation – TB, diarrhoea and other infections

5. Food shortage and malnutrition

  • Undernutrition and anaemia in children and women; also rising obesity

6. Dowry

  • Harassment, domestic violence, dowry deaths, female foeticide; prohibited under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

7. Child labour and child abuse

  • Loss of education and health; exploitation

8. Juvenile delinquency and crime

  • Offences by children and adolescents due to broken homes, poverty, bad company; dealt with under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015

9. Substance abuse

  • Alcoholism and drug addiction (tobacco, cannabis, opioids, inhalants) – family breakdown, accidents, violence, liver and lung disease, HIV through injecting drug use

10. Prostitution and human trafficking

  • Exploitation, STIs and HIV/AIDS

11. HIV/AIDS

  • Health, economic and social effects; stigma and discrimination

12. Domestic violence

  • Physical, emotional, sexual and economic abuse of women

13. Problems of vulnerable groups

  • Elderly – loneliness, neglect, chronic illness
  • Persons with disabilities – discrimination, dependence
  • Minorities and marginal groups – exclusion, poor access to services

14. Other problems – beggary, corruption, communalism, unemployment of educated youth, and the social effects of epidemics such as COVID-19 (job loss, school closures, mental stress)

(c) Role of the nurse (3 marks)

  1. Identification – recognise families and individuals affected during hospital care and home visits (signs of abuse, malnutrition, addiction)
  2. Health education – on nutrition, hygiene, family planning, ill effects of alcohol and tobacco, safe sex, prevention of HIV
  3. Counselling and support – for victims of violence, addicts and their families, people living with HIV, the elderly
  4. Referral – to de-addiction centres, One Stop Centres, child welfare committees, social workers, legal aid and rehabilitation services
  5. Linking with welfare schemes – ICDS, PM-JAY, pensions, Janani Suraksha Yojana, schemes for the disabled
  6. Participating in national health programmes – nutrition, family welfare, AIDS control, tobacco control, mental health
  7. Advocacy – speaking for the rights of vulnerable groups; reporting child abuse and trafficking as required by law
  8. Community participation – working with ASHAs, Anganwadi workers, self-help groups, panchayats and NGOs
  9. Role model – healthy lifestyle, no tobacco or alcohol, respect for all
  10. Research – studying social problems to guide better services

General causes of social problems

  • Poverty, illiteracy, unemployment, rapid population growth, urbanisation and migration, breakdown of the joint family, harmful customs, gender discrimination and weak enforcement of laws

Approaches to solving social problems

  • Legislation, education and awareness, social welfare programmes, voluntary organisations (NGOs), community participation, economic development and empowerment of women

Important laws

Problem Law
Dowry Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
Child marriage Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
Child labour Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2016)
Sexual abuse of children Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012
Domestic violence Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
Trafficking and prostitution Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956
Drug abuse Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985
Juvenile delinquency Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015

Conclusion India faces many social problems – poverty, population growth, illiteracy, dowry, child labour, substance abuse, prostitution, HIV/AIDS and neglect of vulnerable groups. Through identification, education, counselling, referral and advocacy, nurses play an important part in reducing their impact on health.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define social organisation.
answer_html:
Definition Social organisation is the orderly arrangement of the interrelated parts of society – individuals, groups and institutions – so that they work together smoothly to achieve common goals. Ogburn and Nimkoff describe it as an articulation of different parts that perform various functions.

Elements

  1. Individuals and groups
  2. Roles and statuses
  3. Norms and values
  4. Social control
  5. Institutions

Characteristics

  • Orderliness, cooperation, consensus, adjustment and stability

Opposite: social disorganisation – breakdown of this order.

Example: a well-run hospital, where doctors, nurses and other staff have clear roles and rules and cooperate for patient care.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define role. What is role conflict?
answer_html:
Role

  • A role is the expected behaviour attached to a status – the dynamic aspect of status (Ralph Linton)
  • One status carries several roles (a role set) – e.g. a nurse is caregiver, educator, counsellor, advocate and manager

Role conflict

  • Role conflict occurs when a person faces incompatible demands from different roles, or within one role
  • Between roles – a working mother on duty while her child is sick at home
  • Within one role – a nurse expected by patients to spend more time with each, but by the administration to finish work quickly

Reducing role conflict

  • Setting priorities and managing time
  • Family support and flexible duty schedules
  • Clear job descriptions and open discussion with seniors

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Who are the vulnerable groups? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Vulnerable groups are sections of the population who are at greater risk of poverty, discrimination, violence, exploitation and poor health, and who are less able to protect themselves.

Examples

  1. Women – especially pregnant, widowed or deserted women
  2. Children – orphans, street children, child labourers
  3. Elderly people
  4. Persons with disabilities
  5. Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and minorities
  6. Migrant workers, homeless people and slum dwellers
  7. People with mental illness or HIV/AIDS, transgender persons
  8. Disaster victims and refugees
  9. Families below the poverty line

Need: special protection through constitutional provisions, welfare programmes and priority in health services.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What are fundamental duties? Give any four.
answer_html:
Definition Fundamental duties are the moral obligations of every citizen of India. They were added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment (1976) in Article 51A; there are now 11 duties.

Examples

  1. To abide by the Constitution and respect the National Flag and National Anthem
  2. To uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
  3. To promote harmony and brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women
  4. To protect the natural environment – forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife
  5. To develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry
  6. To safeguard public property and abjure violence
  7. Parents to provide opportunities for education to children aged 6–14 years

Note: they are not enforceable by courts, but guide good citizenship.

For nurses: scientific temper against superstition, respect for women and proper biomedical waste disposal.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the role of voluntary organisations in health and welfare.
answer_html:
Introduction Voluntary organisations (non-governmental organisations, NGOs) are non-profit organisations formed voluntarily by people to serve society, independent of government control. They are usually registered as societies or trusts and are funded by donations and grants.

1. Characteristics

  • Voluntary membership and service motive
  • Non-profit and independent
  • Flexible, quick to act and close to the community

2. Important voluntary organisations in India

  • Indian Red Cross Society (1920) – blood banks, first aid, disaster relief
  • Hind Kusht Nivaran Sangh (1950) – leprosy control
  • Tuberculosis Association of India (1939) – TB awareness, TB seals
  • Family Planning Association of India (1949)
  • Kasturba Gandhi National Memorial Trust (1944) – rural women and children
  • Indian Council for Child Welfare (1952)
  • HelpAge India – the elderly; CRY – child rights; SEWA – self-employed women
  • Professional bodies such as the Trained Nurses' Association of India (TNAI)

3. Role in health and welfare

  1. Supplement government services – reach remote and neglected areas
  2. Health education and awareness campaigns
  3. Pioneering services – de-addiction, palliative care, HIV care, mental health
  4. Care of vulnerable groups – orphanages, old-age homes, rehabilitation of persons with disabilities
  5. Disaster relief – food, shelter, medical camps
  6. Advocacy – protect the rights of the poor and press for better policies
  7. Community mobilisation – self-help groups, people's participation
  8. Research and training of volunteers and health workers
  9. Partnership in national health programmes (e.g. TB, HIV and blindness control)

4. Limitations

  • Limited funds and dependence on donors
  • Shortage of trained staff; uneven coverage

5. Role of the nurse

  • Coordinate with voluntary agencies and refer patients for services
  • Volunteer in camps and campaigns
  • Help agencies with health education and training

6. International voluntary agencies

  • Rockefeller Foundation, Ford Foundation, CARE (nutrition and relief), the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) support health work in India and other countries

7. Self-help groups (SHGs)

  • Small groups of 10–20 women from similar backgrounds who save regularly, give small loans to members and take up income-generating work
  • They also spread health awareness – nutrition, sanitation, institutional delivery – and are strong partners for community nurses

Conclusion Voluntary organisations supplement government services through health education, care of vulnerable groups, disaster relief, advocacy and community mobilisation; nurses work with them to extend care to those most in need.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain juvenile delinquency – its causes and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Juvenile delinquency is illegal or antisocial behaviour by a young person below 18 years of age. Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, such a child is called a "child in conflict with law"; the aim is reform and rehabilitation, not punishment.

1. Forms

  • Theft, pickpocketing, vandalism, truancy, gambling
  • Drug use and peddling, violence, gang activity
  • Sexual offences and cyber crimes

2. Causes

  • Family:
    • broken homes, death or desertion of a parent, divorce
    • parental neglect, too strict or too lenient discipline
    • alcoholic or criminal parents, domestic violence
    • poverty and large families
  • Social and environmental:
    • slums and overcrowding, bad company and gangs
    • lack of recreation, migration and urbanisation
  • Economic – poverty, unemployment, child labour, street life
  • Psychological – emotional instability, frustration, low self-esteem, behaviour disorders
  • Educational – school failure, dropout, truancy
  • Mass media – violence in films, the internet and social media
  • Substance abuse

3. Prevention

  • Strengthen the family – parenting education, family counselling
  • School – life-skills education, guidance and counselling, prevention of dropout, sports and cultural activities
  • Recreation – playgrounds, youth clubs, NSS, NCC
  • Poverty alleviation, employment schemes and slum improvement
  • Regulation of media and parental supervision of internet use
  • Early identification of children at risk

4. Legal measures and rehabilitation (JJ Act, 2015)

  • Juvenile Justice Boards decide cases of children in conflict with law
  • Observation homes and special homes; probation and after-care
  • Child Welfare Committees for children in need of care and protection
  • Vocational training and education for reintegration
  • CHILDLINE 1098 for children in difficulty

5. Role of the nurse

  • School health services – identify children with behaviour problems
  • Health education for parents on child-rearing
  • Refer for counselling and de-addiction
  • Work with child welfare agencies

6. Theories in brief

  • Biological – Lombroso believed criminals were "born"; this view is now rejected
  • Psychological – emotional conflicts, frustration and poor conscience development
  • Sociological – differential association (Sutherland): delinquency is learned from close associates; anomie (Merton): gap between goals and the means available

7. Warning signs in a child

  • Truancy, lying, stealing, running away from home
  • Aggression and cruelty; bad company
  • Sudden fall in school performance; substance use

Conclusion Juvenile delinquency arises mainly from family breakdown, poverty, bad company and lack of guidance; it is prevented by strong families, schools, recreation and early help, and managed under the Juvenile Justice Act with a focus on reform.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the problems of persons with disabilities and the welfare measures for them.
answer_html:
Introduction A person with disability is one with a long-term physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairment which, together with barriers in society, prevents full and equal participation. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 recognises 21 types of disability – including blindness, low vision, hearing impairment, locomotor disability, intellectual disability, mental illness, autism, cerebral palsy, thalassaemia, haemophilia, sickle cell disease and acid-attack victims. A disability of 40% or more is a benchmark disability. The 2011 Census counted about 2.7 crore persons with disabilities in India.

A. Problems

  1. Health – secondary complications (pressure sores, contractures, infections), poor access to health care, lack of aids and appliances
  2. Education – low literacy, inaccessible schools, few special educators
  3. Economic – unemployment, poverty, dependence on others
  4. Social – stigma, discrimination, isolation, pity or overprotection; difficulty in marriage
  5. Psychological – low self-esteem, frustration, depression
  6. Accessibility – no ramps, lifts, accessible toilets or transport; information not in Braille or sign language
  7. Vulnerability to abuse – especially women and children with disabilities
  8. Burden on families and caregivers

B. Welfare measures

  • RPwD Act, 2016 – equal rights and non-discrimination; 4% reservation in government jobs and 5% in higher education; free education for children with benchmark disabilities; accessibility of buildings and services
  • Unique Disability ID (UDID) card
  • Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan)
  • ADIP scheme – free aids and appliances (wheelchairs, hearing aids, artificial limbs)
  • Disability pension under the National Social Assistance Programme
  • National Trust – schemes for autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual and multiple disabilities, including health insurance
  • District Disability Rehabilitation Centres; Rehabilitation Council of India
  • Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram and District Early Intervention Centres – early detection of disabilities in children
  • Concessions in travel and income tax

C. Role of the nurse

  • Prevention – antenatal care, immunisation, iodised salt, accident prevention
  • Early detection of developmental delay and referral
  • Rehabilitation – community-based rehabilitation, exercises, prevention of complications
  • Counsel families and fight stigma
  • Help persons get certificates, UDID cards and benefits of schemes

Conclusion Persons with disabilities face health, educational, economic, social and accessibility problems; the RPwD Act and schemes for aids, pensions, reservation and early intervention support them, and nurses play a key role in prevention, rehabilitation and linking them to services.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Discuss alcoholism and drug addiction under the headings: meaning, causes, effects, prevention and role of the nurse. (2 + 3 + 2 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Meaning (2 marks)

  • Alcoholism is a chronic condition marked by uncontrolled drinking, preoccupation with alcohol and continued use despite harm – with tolerance (needing more for the same effect) and withdrawal symptoms when stopped
  • Drug addiction (dependence) is a state of periodic or chronic intoxication, harmful to the individual and society, produced by repeated use of a drug, with a compulsion to continue taking it
  • Physical dependence – the body needs the drug to avoid withdrawal; psychological dependence – craving for its effects
  • Commonly misused substances in India:
    • alcohol – the most common
    • tobacco – smoking and smokeless forms such as gutkha and kharra
    • cannabis – ganja, bhang, charas
    • opioids – heroin (brown sugar, smack), opium, codeine cough syrups
    • sedatives, inhalants (whitener and solvents among street children) and stimulants
  • A national survey (2019) estimated about 16 crore alcohol users, 3.1 crore cannabis users and over 2 crore opioid users in India

(b) Causes (3 marks)

  1. Individual and psychological
    • curiosity, thrill-seeking and peer pressure
    • stress, frustration, loneliness, depression and anxiety
    • low self-esteem; to relieve pain or fatigue (heavy labourers)
  2. Family
    • family history (genetic tendency) and parents who drink or use drugs
    • broken homes, family conflict, neglect; too much pocket money
  3. Social and cultural
    • social acceptance at parties and festivals; traditional drinks (toddy, mahua liquor)
    • easy availability, advertisements and films that glamorise drinking and smoking
    • urbanisation, migration and loss of family control
  4. Economic – unemployment and poverty; also affluence
  5. Occupational – drivers, night-shift and heavy manual workers; easy access to drugs among some workers
  6. Medical – misuse of prescribed painkillers and sleeping pills

(c) Effects (2 marks)

  1. On the individual
    • physical – liver damage (fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis), gastritis, pancreatitis, heart disease, high BP, malnutrition and thiamine deficiency, cancers (mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver), accidents and injuries
    • injecting drug use – HIV, hepatitis B and C, abscesses; risk of overdose and death
    • withdrawal – tremors, sweating, fits and delirium tremens
    • mental – dependence, depression, psychosis, memory loss, personality changes
  2. On the family
    • financial ruin, domestic violence, neglect of children, divorce
    • fetal alcohol syndrome in babies of mothers who drink
  3. On society
    • crime and road traffic accidents (drunken driving)
    • absenteeism and loss of productivity; poverty; burden on health services

(d) Prevention and role of the nurse (3 marks)

Prevention

  • Primary prevention:
    • health education in schools, colleges and workplaces; life-skills training (saying "no", coping with stress)
    • awareness campaigns such as Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan
    • control of availability – licensing, taxes, prohibition in some states and districts, bans on advertising
    • laws – NDPS Act, 1985 (narcotic drugs), COTPA, 2003 (tobacco), penalties for drunken driving
  • Secondary prevention:
    • early identification by screening (e.g. the CAGE questionnaire, AUDIT) and brief advice
    • counselling of early users
  • Tertiary prevention – treatment and rehabilitation:
    • detoxification – safe management of withdrawal under medical care
    • medicines – disulfiram, naltrexone or acamprosate for alcohol; substitution therapy (buprenorphine, methadone) for opioids
    • psychotherapy – motivational interviewing, cognitive behaviour therapy, family therapy
    • self-help groups – Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous; Al-Anon for families
    • rehabilitation – vocational training and follow-up to prevent relapse
    • de-addiction centres and the national de-addiction helpline 14446

Role of the nurse

  • Health educator – teach adolescents, parents and communities about the dangers of substance use
  • Early identification of users in hospitals, schools and the community; non-judgemental approach
  • Motivate the person to accept treatment
  • Care during detoxification:
    • monitor vital signs and withdrawal symptoms (tremors, fits, hallucinations)
    • ensure safety, nutrition and fluids; give thiamine and other medicines as prescribed
  • Counselling and family support; involve the family in treatment
  • Refer to de-addiction centres and self-help groups; follow-up to prevent relapse
  • Rehabilitation – help with return to work and family life
  • Role model – the nurse herself avoids tobacco and alcohol

Stages of alcoholism (Jellinek)

  1. Pre-alcoholic – social drinking to relieve tension
  2. Prodromal – secret drinking, guilt, "blackouts" (memory gaps)
  3. Crucial – loss of control once drinking starts; family and work problems; morning drinking
  4. Chronic – prolonged intoxication, physical and mental deterioration

Warning signs of substance use in adolescents

  • Sudden change in friends, behaviour or school performance
  • Unexplained need for money; missing money or valuables
  • Red eyes, smell of alcohol or smoke, loss of appetite, poor hygiene
  • Secrecy, irritability and withdrawal from family

Conclusion Alcoholism and drug addiction are chronic dependence on substances caused by personal, family, social and economic factors; they damage the individual's health, ruin families and burden society. Prevention needs education, control of supply and early help, and the nurse plays a central role in education, detoxification care, counselling, referral and rehabilitation.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define clinical sociology.
answer_html:
Definition Clinical sociology is the application of sociological knowledge, theories and methods to bring about positive change in the lives of individuals, groups, organisations and communities. It is the "intervention" or applied side of sociology.

Key points

  1. The term was first used by Louis Wirth (1931)
  2. It works at different levels – individual, family, group, organisation, community and society
  3. It focuses on social causes of problems and social solutions
  4. Clinical sociologists work in counselling, health care, crisis intervention, community development and organisational change

subject: Applied Sociology
question: List the uses of clinical sociology.
answer_html:
Uses of clinical sociology

  1. Understanding social causes of illness and behaviour – poverty, family conflict, stigma
  2. Counselling of individuals and families
  3. Crisis intervention – disasters, violence, sudden illness or death
  4. Family therapy and conflict resolution
  5. Developing services for the abused – women, children, the elderly
  6. Rehabilitation of addicts, prisoners, disabled and mentally ill persons
  7. Organisational development – improving teamwork in hospitals
  8. Community development and health promotion programmes
  9. Policy planning and evaluation of social programmes

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain the use of clinical sociology in crisis intervention.
answer_html:
Introduction A crisis is a sudden, stressful event that disturbs a person's normal balance and with which the person cannot cope using usual methods (Gerald Caplan). Crisis intervention is short-term, immediate help to restore the person to at least the previous level of functioning. Clinical sociology adds the social dimension – family, social support, community resources and culture.

1. Types of crisis

  • Maturational (developmental) – normal life transitions: adolescence, marriage, parenthood, retirement
  • Situational – unexpected events: sudden illness, accident, death of a loved one, job loss, divorce
  • Adventitious (social) – disasters, riots, war, epidemics, violence

2. Phases of a crisis

  1. Rising tension when the usual coping fails
  2. Increasing anxiety and disorganisation
  3. Mobilisation of emergency coping resources
  4. If unresolved – breakdown (depression, panic, suicidal thoughts)

3. Steps of crisis intervention

  1. Assessment – the event, its meaning to the person, coping ability, support systems, risk of harm
  2. Planning – short-term goals with the person and family
  3. Intervention – reduce anxiety, help the person understand the situation, explore coping methods, mobilise support
  4. Resolution – check that the person is coping
  5. Anticipatory planning – prepare for future stress

4. Contribution of clinical sociology

  • Social support networks – family, friends, neighbours, religious groups and community organisations are mobilised to support the person
  • Family-level intervention – the whole family is affected by a crisis and is helped together
  • Cultural understanding – culture shapes how people grieve, seek help and express distress
  • Community resources – linking with shelters, helplines, self-help groups, welfare schemes and legal aid
  • Group and community crisis – organising group debriefing and community support after disasters
  • Reducing stigma – helping communities accept victims (of violence, HIV, suicide attempts)

5. Role of the nurse

  • Stay with the person, listen and give emotional support
  • Ensure safety (risk of suicide or violence)
  • Give clear, simple information
  • Involve family and support groups; refer to counsellors and helplines (e.g. Tele-MANAS 14416, women's helpline 181, CHILDLINE 1098)
  • Follow up

Conclusion Crisis intervention gives immediate help to people overwhelmed by stressful events; clinical sociology strengthens it by using family, community and cultural resources to support recovery.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Define clinical sociology. Explain its scope and the sociological strategies for developing services for the abused. (2 + 3 + 5)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Clinical sociology is the applied branch of sociology that uses sociological knowledge, perspectives and methods to assess and intervene in social problems, so as to bring about positive change for individuals, groups, organisations and communities
  • The term was introduced by Louis Wirth (1931)
  • While general sociology tries to understand society, clinical sociology tries to change it – like the clinical side of medicine

(b) Scope of clinical sociology (3 marks)

  1. Individual level – counselling, life-skills training, rehabilitation of addicts, prisoners and people with disability or mental illness
  2. Family level – family therapy, marital counselling, help in domestic violence and family crises
  3. Group level – support groups, self-help groups, group therapy
  4. Organisational level – improving communication, teamwork and conflict resolution in hospitals, schools and industries
  5. Community level – community development, health promotion, disaster relief, rehabilitation after riots or disasters
  6. Societal level – social policy, planning and evaluation of welfare programmes, advocacy for vulnerable groups
  7. In health care – understanding social causes of disease, patient compliance, stigma and health-seeking behaviour

(c) Sociological strategies for developing services for the abused (5 marks)

Who are the abused? Women facing domestic or sexual violence, abused or neglected children, abused elderly people, persons with disabilities, trafficked persons and victims of caste or communal violence.

1. Understanding the problem (needs assessment)

  • Study the extent, causes and pattern of abuse in the community – surveys, records, interviews
  • Identify risk factors – alcohol misuse, poverty, dowry demands, gender inequality, social isolation
  • Understand cultural beliefs that make abuse acceptable or hidden (family honour, fear of stigma)

2. Early identification and screening

  • Train health workers, teachers, police and ASHAs to recognise signs of abuse
  • Routine, private screening for violence in antenatal clinics, emergency departments and paediatric wards

3. Crisis and emergency services

  • One Stop Centres (Sakhi) – medical aid, police help, legal aid, counselling and temporary shelter for women under one roof
  • Helplines – 181 (women), 1098 (CHILDLINE), 14567 (elderly)
  • Emergency medical care, medico-legal examination and evidence collection with consent

4. Shelter and protection

  • Short-stay homes and shelter homes (Swadhar Greh), child care institutions
  • Protection orders under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005; protection under the POCSO Act, 2012 and the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007

5. Counselling and psychosocial support

  • Individual and family counselling; trauma-informed care
  • Support groups where survivors share experiences and regain confidence

6. Legal aid and justice

  • Free legal aid through Legal Services Authorities
  • Help in filing complaints and following cases; child-friendly courts

7. Empowerment and rehabilitation

  • Education, vocational training, employment and self-help groups for economic independence
  • Help with housing and reintegration with family or community

8. Coordination between sectors (multi-agency approach)

  • Health, police, legal, social welfare, education departments and NGOs working together with clear referral pathways

9. Prevention and community awareness

  • Public education campaigns against dowry, child marriage, alcohol abuse and violence
  • Gender sensitisation in schools; involving men and community leaders
  • Changing social norms that tolerate violence

10. Training, research and policy

  • Training of professionals in sensitive handling of survivors
  • Research to evaluate services; advocacy for better laws and budgets

Role of the nurse

  • Identify and document abuse carefully; maintain confidentiality and privacy
  • Provide first aid, medical care and emotional support
  • Report as required by law (mandatory in child sexual abuse)
  • Refer to One Stop Centres, counsellors, legal aid and shelters
  • Educate communities and take part in prevention programmes

Conclusion Clinical sociology applies sociological knowledge to solve social problems at every level. For the abused, it guides the development of complete services – identification, crisis help, shelter, counselling, legal aid, rehabilitation and prevention – delivered through coordination among health, police, legal and welfare agencies.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: What is elder abuse? List its types.
answer_html:
Definition Elder abuse is a single or repeated act, or lack of appropriate action, occurring within any relationship where there is an expectation of trust, which causes harm or distress to an older person (WHO).

Types

  1. Physical – hitting, pushing, improper restraint
  2. Psychological (emotional) – insults, threats, humiliation, isolation
  3. Financial (material) – taking money or property, forcing the person to sign documents
  4. Sexual abuse
  5. Neglect – not providing food, medicines, hygiene or care
  6. Abandonment and violation of rights

Risk factors: dependence, dementia, caregiver stress, substance use by the caregiver, property disputes.

Protection: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; national helpline for senior citizens Elderline 14567.

Nursing: recognise signs (unexplained injuries, malnutrition, fear of caregivers), document, report and support.

subject: Applied Sociology
question: Explain domestic violence – its causes, effects and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Domestic violence is any act of physical, sexual, verbal, emotional or economic abuse by a member of the household, usually by the husband or in-laws against a woman; it also includes child and elder abuse. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA), 2005 defines and covers all these forms. National Family Health Survey data show that nearly 3 in 10 married women have experienced violence by their husbands.

1. Forms

  • Physical – beating, burning, choking
  • Sexual – forced sexual acts
  • Verbal and emotional – insults, threats, humiliation, isolation, controlling behaviour
  • Economic – denying money, taking away earnings, preventing work
  • Dowry harassment

2. Causes

  • Patriarchal attitudes, gender inequality and acceptance of violence as "normal"
  • Alcoholism and drug use of the husband
  • Dowry demands
  • Economic dependence of women; poverty, unemployment, financial stress
  • Suspicion and jealousy; infertility; son preference
  • Having witnessed violence in childhood; low education
  • Conflicts in the joint family

3. Effects

  • Physical – injuries, fractures, burns, chronic pain, unwanted pregnancy, abortion, sexually transmitted infections, low birth weight, and even death (dowry deaths)
  • Mental – fear, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, low self-esteem
  • On children – fear, behaviour problems, poor school performance, and the cycle of violence in the next generation
  • Social and economic – isolation, loss of work, family breakdown

4. Legal protection and services

  • PWDVA, 2005 – Protection Officers; protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief and custody orders
  • Cruelty by the husband or his relatives is a criminal offence (Section 498A of the IPC, now Sections 85–86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023); Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
  • One Stop Centres (Sakhi), Women Helpline 181, emergency number 112, family counselling centres and shelter homes

5. Role of the nurse

  • Recognise signs – repeated injuries with unconvincing explanations, delay in seeking care, fear of the partner, depression
  • Ask privately and sensitively ("Has anyone hurt you?"); listen without judging; believe and support her
  • Treat injuries and document them carefully (medico-legal record)
  • Maintain privacy and confidentiality; help with a safety plan
  • Inform her of her rights and refer to One Stop Centres, counselling, legal aid and shelters
  • Community education – involve men and boys, promote gender equality, support self-help groups for women

Conclusion Domestic violence, mainly against women, arises from patriarchy, alcohol, dowry and economic dependence, and harms the physical and mental health of women and children; the law provides protection, and the nurse plays a vital role in identification, care, documentation and referral.
